README.md.overview: The project's front door: what Fiu is (a CLI that turns real repository code into small, Verified practice exercises called Workouts), the five Workout kinds, how to install and start, and the principles it never breaks. It is the first stop of the tour because every later file implements something promised here, from the sandbox to the Atlas to agent mode.

sections.title: Pitch and comprehension debt
sections.explanation: Introduces the name (from Italian *fiuto*, a nose for it) and the problem Fiu targets: *comprehension debt* from code written by AI agents. The key promise is that exercises are **Verified**, which is the thread later tied to the Verified Gate.

sections.title: The five Workout kinds
sections.explanation: A table splits Workouts into editor-based kinds (Drill, Kata) and terminal-only kinds (Prediction, What-if, Diagnosis), each with the command that starts it. It then explains how `fiu train` copies code into `.fiu/attempts/<id>/<n>/`, how `$VISUAL` is spawned detached, what the Debrief and "Around this code" are, and the optional Understand-Anything integration. The last paragraph states the core invariant: answers are measured by running code in an OS sandbox, never asserted by the model.

sections.title: Quick start and workflows
sections.explanation: Shows the install path (`npm install && npm run build && npm link`) and the typical first session: `fiu init`, `fiu atlas build`, `fiu drill`, `fiu train`. The agent-mode alternative (`fiu agent install claude`) avoids needing an API key. The workflow list maps each remaining subcommand (atlas, explore/track, quick, map, stats, share/fetch, auto, cost) to its purpose, which mirrors the command registrations in `src/cli.ts`.

sections.title: Principles and requirements
sections.explanation: Five principles (non-blocking, zero repo pollution, untrusted generated code, no telemetry, called by agents rather than driving them) explain many design choices you will see in code, such as hiding `.fiu/` via `.git/info/exclude`. Requirements list Node.js 22.18+ (matching `engines` in package.json), Linux/macOS, and the per-language toolchains.

sections.title: Tutorials, history, license
sections.explanation: Links to a blog tutorial series, then notes the project's former names (Fiutsu, Kintsugi) and that the first run migrates old state automatically, which is what the `preAction` hook in `src/cli.ts` does. Ends with the Apache-2.0 license.

GLOSSARY.md.overview: The ubiquitous-language glossary: every domain term used in code, prompts, and docs, each with a precise definition and an *Avoid* list of synonyms not to use. Reading it alongside the README (tour step 1) makes identifiers like `Workout`, `Attempt`, `Series`, `Track`, and `Verified` unambiguous throughout the codebase.

sections.title: Purpose statement
sections.explanation: A one-sentence definition of Fiu that frames everything below: a CLI turning code from the developer's own repository into small, verified practice exercises.

sections.title: Exercise kinds and groupings
sections.explanation: Defines Workout (an immutable definition) versus Attempt (one try, owning the outcome), then each kind: Kata, Drill, Prediction, Diagnosis, What-if, plus Proposed Change. Series and Track are explicitly *not* Workouts but groupings of them. Atlas, Link, and Atlas Entry describe the repository map, with Links computed by Fiu (imports, co-change) rather than written by a model. Quick is a size constraint, not a kind.

sections.title: Anatomy of a Workout
sections.explanation: Names every part of a Workout: Around this code and Debrief (assembled by Fiu, never by the generating model), Starting Code, Reference Solution, Scenario, Previous Version, Variant, Cause, Symptom, Hint, Source Anchor, Origin, Generator, Regression Test. The Verified entry is the formal acceptance rule the Verified Gate implements: the reference passes every test, and the Starting Code runs but fails at least one test by assertion while passing another.

sections.title: Languages and progress
sections.explanation: Language Profile is the abstraction that keeps the core language-agnostic. The Progress terms (Completed, Abandoned, Practised, Stale, Blind Spot, Discarded) define the outcomes and coverage concepts used by the runner, `fiu map`, and `fiu stats`; note the careful distinction between Discarded and expired, and that editing tests to pass does not count as Completed.

SPEC.md.overview: The full product specification: vision, principles, packaging, CLI surface, Language Profiles, the Verified Gate, the sandbox threat model and policy, the generation pipeline, workspace layout, and a long release plan describing each later feature (queue, background generation, Tracks, map, Katas, Predictions, Atlas, Diagnosis, Debrief). Tour step 2 uses it as the authoritative reference that the source modules cite by section number (e.g. `§11.2.4` in `config.ts`).

sections.title: Vision and principles
sections.explanation: States the long-term vision and that v1 shipped exactly one workflow (`fiu drill`). The principles section is stricter than the README's: standard-library-only Workouts, nothing unverified reaches the user, the LLM never chooses what runs (commands come only from Language Profiles), secrets never live in the repo, and answers are measured, each linked to an ADR.

sections.title: Packaging and former names
sections.explanation: A table fixes the package, binary, Node runtime (22.18+ for native type-stripping), platforms, the pinned sandbox runtime, and the orchestrator stack, matching `package.json`. Section 3.1 tabulates every on-disk name moved from Fiutsu/Kintsugi to Fiu and which command moves it.

sections.title: CLI reference
sections.explanation: One row per command with its flags and the spec section that defines it. It is the contract that `src/cli.ts` implements with commander; useful for checking which options each subcommand should accept.

sections.title: Language Profiles
sections.explanation: Describes the per-language abstraction (file matching, test command, result parsing), the built-in profiles, and how users declare their own in config. This is the design behind `src/languages/`.

sections.title: Verified Gate and sandbox
sections.explanation: Section 6 lists the gate's checks (reference passes, Starting Code fails meaningfully, Drill regression test, minimal diff) and the retry policy of up to two more generations with failure feedback. Section 7 gives the threat model, the per-run policy table (no network, restricted writes and reads, scrubbed environment), the three resource-limit layers with the rejected cgroups approach, the canary, and behavior when no sandbox is available.

sections.title: Generation pipeline and LLM schema
sections.explanation: Section 8 is the step-by-step generation flow: resolve target, preflight, consent, synthesize, verify, persist, train. Section 9 defines the structured LLM output schema and prompt rules the synthesis code follows.

sections.title: Workspace and runner
sections.explanation: Shows the `.fiu/` layout (config.json, state.json, workouts/, attempts/) that `src/workspace.ts` encodes, the rule that API keys come only from environment variables or `~/.config/fiu/`, the runner's behavior and keys ([h], [g], [q], Ctrl+C), and the `state.json` outcomes and spend ledger format.

sections.title: Release plan
sections.explanation: A versioned history of features beyond v1, each marked implemented or not: agent mode, cost visibility, Workouts/Attempts, the queue and `fiu quick`, background generation, Tracks, team sharing, `fiu map`, Katas, real bugs, Predictions, the Atlas, Series, calibration and Blind Spots, Diagnosis, What-ifs, and Links/Debrief. Code comments elsewhere reference these subsections directly.

sections.title: Implementation roadmaps
sections.explanation: Brief roadmaps for v1, v2, and v3 summarizing the order in which the pieces were built.

package.json.overview: The npm manifest. It declares the `fiu` binary (pointing at the compiled `dist/cli.js`), requires Node.js 22.18+, defines build/typecheck/test scripts, and lists the small runtime stack named in SPEC section 3. Tour step 2 pairs it with the tsconfig files to show how the TypeScript sources become a runnable CLI.

sections.title: Identity and binary
sections.explanation: The package is `private` (the spec notes the npm name is taken) and ESM (`"type": "module"`). `bin.fiu` maps the command to `dist/cli.js`, and only `dist` is published via `files`. The `engines` floor of Node 22.18 is what allows running `.ts` sources directly in tests.

sections.title: Scripts
sections.explanation: `build` compiles with `tsconfig.build.json`, `typecheck` runs `tsc --noEmit` over src and test, and `test` uses Node's built-in test runner with `--experimental-strip-types`, so tests run straight from TypeScript without a build step.

sections.title: Dependencies
sections.explanation: Runtime deps: the Vercel AI SDK (`ai`) plus Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI providers; `@anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime` pinned to an exact version (the spec requires it pinned since sandbox behavior is security-critical); `commander` and `@clack/prompts` for the CLI; `execa` for subprocesses; `zod` for schemas; and the MCP SDK for agent mode. Dev deps are only TypeScript and Node types.

tsconfig.json.overview: The base TypeScript configuration used for typechecking both `src` and `test`. Its options are chosen so the same `.ts` files can run directly under Node's type-stripping and also compile to `dist`. Part of tour step 2's build setup.

sections.title: Compiler options
sections.explanation: Targets ES2023 with `nodenext` module resolution and strict checking, plus `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` (which is why the code uses `!` on array indexes like `listing[0]!`). `erasableSyntaxOnly` and `verbatimModuleSyntax` forbid TypeScript-only runtime constructs (enums, parameter properties) and require `import type`, so Node can strip types without transforming code. `allowImportingTsExtensions` with `rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` lets sources import `./x.ts` while the compiled output imports `./x.js`.

sections.title: Included files
sections.explanation: Includes both `src` and `test`, so `npm run typecheck` covers the tests too; the build config narrows this.

tsconfig.build.json.overview: The build-only TypeScript config: it extends the base config and emits only the `src` tree into `dist`, which is what the `bin` entry in package.json points to. Part of tour step 2.

sections.title: Build overrides
sections.explanation: Extends `./tsconfig.json`, sets `rootDir` to `src` and `outDir` to `dist`, and restricts `include` to `src` so tests are not emitted. Keeping `rootDir` as `src` makes `src/cli.ts` land at `dist/cli.js`, and keeps `src/version.ts` and `dist/version.js` at the same depth relative to package.json.

src/version.ts.overview: A tiny module exporting Fiu's version string, read from package.json at runtime. The CLI uses it for `--version`, and agent mode stamps it into installed files and the MCP server. Part of tour step 3.

sections.title: Reading the version
sections.explanation: Resolves `../package.json` relative to `import.meta.url` and parses its `version`. Because both `src/version.ts` and the compiled `dist/version.js` sit one level below the package root, the same relative URL works whether running from source or from the build, so there is a single source of truth for the version.

src/terminal.ts.overview: The real-terminal implementation of the `TrainIo` interface that the training runner depends on. It handles raw-mode key reading, the Workout picker, ratings, defect confirmation, launching `$VISUAL`, and waiting spinners. Keeping this behind an interface lets `commands/train.ts` stay testable while `src/cli.ts` injects the real terminal (tour step 3).

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Pulls in `spawn` for the editor, readline's `emitKeypressEvents`, clack prompts, the `TrainIo` type from the train command, cost formatting, and `shellQuote` from the sandbox process helpers.

sections.title: NotInteractiveError
sections.explanation: A dedicated error thrown when stdin is not a TTY, so training fails with a clear message rather than hanging on keypresses that will never arrive.

sections.title: KeyReader
sections.explanation: Wraps stdin in raw mode and turns keypress events into single key names, mapping Ctrl+C to `q` (matching the spec's rule that Ctrl+C behaves like quit). Each `read()` registers a waiter; a keypress resolves all current waiters at once and clears them. An optional `AbortSignal` removes the waiter and resolves `undefined`, letting the runner race key input against other events such as file saves. `close()` restores cooked mode and pauses stdin.

sections.title: terminalTrainIo factory and picker
sections.explanation: Throws `NotInteractiveError` up front without a TTY. The `KeyReader` is created lazily (`keys ??= ...`) because the clack `select` picker needs cooked mode, and it runs before any key reading begins. The picker labels Series questions with their position and shows hints for open Attempts and generation cost.

sections.title: Rating and defect prompts
sections.explanation: Both read one raw key: `y`/`n` map to a value and anything else skips (`undefined`). `rate` feeds the local Workout rating; `confirmDefect` asks whether a finding is a real bug in the user's code (the "real bugs" feature).

sections.title: Editor, waiting, and close
sections.explanation: `openEditor` spawns `$VISUAL` detached with stdio ignored and `unref()`, so a GUI editor opens without stealing the terminal; file paths are shell-quoted since the command runs with `shell: true`. `wait` shows a spinner whose message is refreshed every second from a status callback until a promise settles, always clearing the timer in `finally`. `close` restores the terminal only if a reader was ever created.

src/cli.ts.overview: The executable entry point (`#!/usr/bin/env node`, compiled to `dist/cli.js`). It builds the whole `fiu` command tree with commander, translates each command's result object into terminal messages and exit codes, and injects terminal UIs into the command modules. Business logic lives in `src/commands/` and other modules; many are loaded lazily with dynamic `import()` so each invocation only pays for what it uses. This is the centrepiece of tour step 3.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Eagerly imports only what the common paths need: commander, clack prompts, the drill/train/init commands, cost formatting, workspace and config helpers, the legacy migration, and `VERSION`. Heavier or rarer modules (MCP SDK, atlas, background refill, explore) are imported dynamically inside their actions.

sections.title: Root program and migration hook
sections.explanation: Creates the root command with name, description, and `--version` from `version.ts`. A `preAction` hook runs before every command to migrate state from the former names (Fiutsu, Kintsugi); failures are printed but never block the command, honouring the non-blocking principle.

sections.title: fiu init
sections.explanation: Delegates to `commands/init.ts`, then reports whether the workspace was created, whether `.fiu/` was added to `.git/info/exclude`, and the sandbox canary result. A sandbox problem sets `process.exitCode = 1` rather than throwing, so the remaining tips still print.

sections.title: Shared generation flow
sections.explanation: `trackKindList` and `questionCount` are commander option parsers that validate input and throw readable errors. `generationCommand(kind)` returns one action reused by drill, kata, predict, and diagnose: it runs `drill()` with a spinner UI, then branches on the result status (`not-worth-practicing`, `failed`, or saved, possibly as a Series). On success it either opens the runner directly (only with a TTY and without `--no-train`) or prints kind-specific next steps.

sections.title: Generation commands
sections.explanation: Registers `drill`, `kata`, `predict`, and `diagnose` with matching flags (`--quick`, `--no-train`, `-y`, `--no-sandbox`). `predict` adds `--commit`, `--what-if`, and `--questions`, and validates incompatible combinations before routing: without `--commit` it uses the shared flow, with `--commit` it goes through `runRefill` restricted to the `prediction` kind.

sections.title: Agent mode commands and helpers
sections.explanation: `fiu mcp` lazily loads the MCP SDK and serves over stdio; the comment notes stdout carries the protocol so nothing else may print to it. `agent install/uninstall` call the Claude Code installer and report written/removed files, falling back to a manual MCP registration command. `fiuCommand()` rebuilds the exact way to re-launch this same `fiu` (node path, exec args, real script path) so hooks and agents do not depend on PATH.

sections.title: Cost, Tracks, sharing, and map
sections.explanation: `cost` reports spend since a date; `explore` builds a Track from a directory or an `--about` goal (exactly one is required) and reports dropped, insufficient, or saved Tracks; `track` lists Tracks or continues one via `runTrack`, opening a single Track directly only when there is a terminal. `share`, `fetch`, and `map` follow the same pattern of a lazily imported command plus result formatting.

sections.title: Atlas and stats
sections.explanation: The `atlas` group has `show` (the default subcommand, text or Markdown), `search` (local ranking with state markers and suggested `fiu drill` targets, noting when only names are matched or results come from Understand-Anything), and `build` (describes stale or missing entries and reports cost and failures). Colour is enabled only for a TTY without `NO_COLOR`. `stats` follows.

sections.title: Queue and background generation
sections.explanation: `quick` serves the best Quick Workout, optionally `--while` a command runs; `refill` and the `auto on/off/status` group manage background generation from commits, including validating caps and installing the post-commit hook (or printing a snippet when `core.hooksPath` is set). `runRefill` stays fully silent with `--background`, logging only to `.fiu/log`. `quickWhileCommand` never blocks the user's command: without a TTY, repository, or workspace, or with nothing ready, it just runs the command in the foreground and propagates its exit code.

sections.title: Train, archive, UI, and main
sections.explanation: `train` shows unseen background failures then calls `runTrain`, which always closes the terminal IO in `finally`. `discard` handles Series ids specially; `restore` reverses it. `terminalUi()` implements `DrillUi`, showing each step as a spinner until the next one and offering `confirm` only with a TTY. The file ends with a top-level `await program.parseAsync()` wrapped so any thrown error prints as `fiu: <message>` with exit code 1 instead of a stack trace.

src/workspace.ts.overview: Defines and manages the per-repository `.fiu/` workspace: locating the git root, computing every workspace path, creating missing files without overwriting, and hiding the workspace from git through the repo-local exclude file. It encodes the zero-repo-pollution principle and is used by almost every command (tour step 4).

sections.title: Constants and path shape
sections.explanation: `WORKSPACE_DIRNAME` is `.fiu`, and the exclude line is anchored at the repository root (`/.fiu/`). `WorkspacePaths` names every location Fiu uses: config, state, workouts, attempts, the Atlas and its cached links, plus the v1 `done` folder that is kept only so legacy notices can find it.

sections.title: Finding the repository
sections.explanation: `findRepoRoot` runs `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` with `reject: false` and turns a non-zero exit into `NotAGitRepositoryError`, giving users a clear instruction instead of a raw git error.

sections.title: Computing paths
sections.explanation: `workspacePaths` is a pure function mapping a repo root to all workspace paths, so callers compute locations consistently without touching the disk.

sections.title: Creating the workspace
sections.explanation: `ensureWorkspace` creates `workouts/` recursively and seeds `config.json` (`{}`) and `state.json` (`{ outcomes: [] }`) only if missing. It returns whether the workspace root was new, which `fiu init` uses to word its message. Idempotency lets other commands such as `fiu auto on` call it safely.

sections.title: Hiding from git
sections.explanation: Adds a pattern to `info/exclude` instead of the tracked `.gitignore`, so Fiu never edits tracked files. The path is resolved with `git rev-parse --git-path`, which handles worktrees and custom `GIT_DIR`s. Existing lines are compared after trimming, including equivalent spellings (`.fiu/`), and a newline separator is inserted only when the file does not already end with one.

sections.title: Tracked check and safe write
sections.explanation: `isTracked` uses `git ls-files --error-unmatch` to ask whether git tracks a path, supporting the rule that Fiu never modifies tracked files. `writeIfMissing` uses the exclusive `wx` flag and swallows only `EEXIST`, an atomic create-if-absent with no race between checking and writing.

src/config.ts.overview: Loads, validates, and merges Fiu's two configuration files: the repository-level `.fiu/config.json` (never secrets) and the user-level `~/.config/fiu/config.json` (the only place API keys may live). Zod schemas give strict validation with readable errors, and `resolveConfig` produces the effective non-secret settings with repo values overriding user values overriding defaults. Tour step 4 covers it with the workspace and consent.

sections.title: Imports, providers, and defaults
sections.explanation: Declares the three supported providers as a `const` tuple feeding a Zod enum, the background-generation caps (`AUTO_DEFAULTS`), and the default provider and model, checked with `satisfies Partial<ResolvedConfig>`. `KindsSchema` lists the kinds `fiu quick` can favour and commits can become; Katas are excluded because they are made only on request.

sections.title: Repository config schema
sections.explanation: `z.strictObject` rejects unknown keys, catching typos. The repo config holds provider/model, the recorded consent (provider plus timestamp), user-defined Language Profiles, price overrides, preferred kinds, the `context` and `understandAnything` toggles, the sharing remote, and the `auto` block with its consent time and caps. It deliberately has no `apiKeys` field, since this file lives inside the repository.

sections.title: User config schema
sections.explanation: The user config is the only schema with `apiKeys`, a partial record keyed by provider. It also carries kinds and `predictionQuestions`, bounded by `MAX_SERIES_QUESTIONS` from the synthesis schema.

sections.title: Resolved config and errors
sections.explanation: `ResolvedConfig` is the merged shape the rest of the app consumes, with comments documenting each field's precedence. `ConfigError` marks user-fixable config problems. `userConfigPath` and `userCacheDir` honour `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` and `XDG_CACHE_HOME`, and take an injectable `ConfigEnv` so tests can point them at a fake home.

sections.title: Loading the two files
sections.explanation: A missing file means an empty config. `loadRepoConfig` checks for `apiKeys` before schema parsing so the user gets a targeted message (use an env var or the user config) rather than a generic unknown-key error.

sections.title: Merging settings
sections.explanation: `resolveConfig` uses `??` chains for repo over user over defaults, merges price maps with repo entries spreading last, combines built-in and declared Language Profiles via the registry, defaults kinds to `['drill']`, and turns "Around this code" on unless the repo disables it. Secrets are intentionally not part of the resolved object.

sections.title: JSON and schema helpers
sections.explanation: `readJson` returns `undefined` for missing files and wraps JSON syntax errors in a `ConfigError` naming the file. `parse` uses `safeParse` and `z.prettifyError` so validation failures read as a list of problems tied to the file path.

src/credentials.ts.overview: Resolves the API key for the configured LLM provider. It is a small but security-relevant foundation module: keys may only come from environment variables or the user-level config file, never from repository config. Tour step 4 groups it with workspace, config and consent as the guardrails every model-calling command passes through.

sections.title: Provider env var map
sections.explanation: Imports the `Provider`, `UserConfig` and `ConfigEnv` types plus `userConfigPath` from config.ts. `API_KEY_ENV_VARS` is a `Record<Provider, string>`, so TypeScript forces an entry for every supported provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google). The variable names match the conventions of each vendor's SDK.

sections.title: MissingApiKeyError
sections.explanation: A dedicated error type whose message tells the user exactly how to fix the problem: which environment variable to set, or which JSON snippet to add to the user config file (whose path comes from `userConfigPath`). Callers can catch it by class to show a friendly message instead of a stack trace.

sections.title: resolveApiKey
sections.explanation: Looks up the key with a simple precedence: the environment variable first, then `user.apiKeys[provider]`. Note it takes only the user-level config, never the repo config, which is how the 'no secrets in the repo' rule is enforced structurally rather than by convention. The `||` means an empty-string env var falls through to the config file.

src/consent.ts.overview: Implements Fiu's explicit consent rule: before any code from a repository is sent to an LLM provider, the user must agree, and that agreement is recorded in `.fiu/config.json`. Consent is tracked per repository and per provider. It is part of tour step 4's foundation layer, checked by commands like drill before any model call.

sections.title: Consent error types
sections.explanation: Two errors model the two ways consent can be missing. `ConsentRequiredError` is thrown in non-interactive contexts and tells the user to re-run interactively or pass `--yes`; `ConsentDeclinedError` reports that the user said no and reassures them nothing was sent.

sections.title: hasConsent
sections.explanation: Consent is granted only when the stored `consent.provider` equals the provider about to be used. Switching from one provider to another therefore asks again, because the user agreed to share code with a specific vendor, not with any vendor.

sections.title: recordConsent
sections.explanation: Reads the raw JSON of the repo config (or starts from an empty object), sets `consent` to the provider and an ISO timestamp, and writes the file back pretty-printed. It deliberately works on the raw object rather than a parsed `RepoConfig` so unknown or defaulted fields are preserved exactly as the user wrote them. The injectable `now` parameter makes the timestamp testable.

src/languages/profile.ts.overview: Defines the Language Profile schema: the pure-data description of everything Fiu needs to generate, build and run Workouts in one language. It also defines the normalized `TestRun` shape every runner produces and the Zod schema for user-declared profiles in config. Tour step 5 starts here because builtin.ts, registry.ts, run.ts and parsers.ts all build on these types.

sections.title: Result formats and import styles
sections.explanation: `ResultFormat` enumerates the test-output formats Fiu knows how to parse (TAP, JUnit XML, Go's JSON events, unittest verbose output). `IMPORT_STYLES` is declared as a `const` tuple so the same list feeds both the `ImportStyle` type and the Zod enum later, avoiding duplicated literals.

sections.title: LanguageProfile interface
sections.explanation: The central data type. Fields cover file naming (`codeFilename`, `testFilename`, `supportFiles`), Atlas hints (`declarationPattern`, `importStyle`, `lineComment`), LLM guidance (`promptRules`), toolchain commands (`preflightCmd`, `warmup`, `testCmd`) and result parsing (`resultFormat`, `resultFile`). The sandbox-related fields are notable: profiles can add env vars, cache dirs and extra read/write paths, but the comments stress there is deliberately no way to allow network access, and `limits` can be tuned but never switched off.

sections.title: Normalized test results
sections.explanation: `TestResult` and `TestRun` are the language-neutral output of a test run. `outcome` distinguishes passing tests, assertion failures and other errors, which matters for the Verified Gate. `ran: false` means tests never executed (compile/import failure or a stop), and `stopped` records whether Fiu killed the run for timeout, memory or process count. `output` is kept for both humans and LLM retry feedback.

sections.title: relativePath validator
sections.explanation: A reusable Zod refinement for file paths inside the Workout directory: non-empty, not absolute and with no `..` segment. It prevents a config-declared profile from writing files outside the Workout.

sections.title: UserProfileSchema
sections.explanation: The strict Zod schema for profiles declared in config. It mirrors `LanguageProfile` but adds validation: ids are lowercase slugs, extensions look like `.rs`, `declarationPattern` must compile as a RegExp and contain a `(?<name>` group, and env var names are checked. Importantly, `resultFormat` only allows `tap` and `junit-xml`, the machine-readable, language-neutral formats, while the built-in-only formats stay internal. Read/write paths must be absolute, and `strictObject` rejects unknown keys.

src/languages/builtin.ts.overview: Declares the four built-in Language Profiles: TypeScript, JavaScript, Python and Go. Each is a plain object conforming to `LanguageProfile`, which shows the 'profiles are pure data' design in practice. The registry (tour step 5) merges these with any profiles declared in config.

sections.title: Shared prompt rules and base
sections.explanation: `SHARED_RULES` holds LLM constraints common to every language: standard library only, one code file and one test file. `NO_JSX` is reused by the JS-family profiles. `base` supplies empty defaults for the sandbox-related fields so each profile only spells out what differs.

sections.title: TypeScript profile
sections.explanation: Runs TypeScript directly with Node's type stripping and the built-in `node:test` runner with TAP output. The prompt rules require erasable-only syntax (no enums, namespaces, parameter properties or decorators), because type stripping cannot compile those. The comment explains why `--experimental-strip-types` is still passed: it is a no-op on newer Node but lets older 22.x releases run Workouts.

sections.title: JavaScript profile
sections.explanation: Uses `.mjs` files so ES modules work without a package.json, and the same `node --test` TAP reporter as TypeScript. The preflight is just `node --version`, since no extra toolchain is needed.

sections.title: Python profile
sections.explanation: Uses `unittest` in verbose mode, whose results are parsed from stderr by the `unittest-verbose` parser. `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE` keeps `__pycache__` files out of the Workout directory.

sections.title: Go profile
sections.explanation: The most involved profile. It ships a `go.mod` as a support file, warms the build cache during preflight with a trivial test (a cold build of `testing` takes about 8 s, close to the 10 s run timeout), and parses `go test -json`. The env block disables the module proxy, toolchain downloads and workspaces so Go never reaches for the network inside the sandbox, and `GOCACHE` is mapped to a persistent per-user cache directory.

sections.title: Built-in list
sections.explanation: `BUILTIN_PROFILES` is the ordered, readonly list the registry falls back to after user-declared profiles.

src/languages/registry.ts.overview: Combines built-in and config-declared Language Profiles into one list and picks the profile for a given source file by extension. It is the lookup point other modules use to decide how a Workout should be generated and run, as described in tour step 5.

sections.title: UnsupportedLanguageError
sections.explanation: Thrown when no profile claims a file's extension. The message lists every supported extension and points the user to declaring their own profile in config, turning a dead end into a hint.

sections.title: profiles merge
sections.explanation: Builds the effective profile list with clear precedence: repo-declared profiles, then user-declared, then built-ins. A profile whose id is already present is skipped, so a declared profile replaces a built-in of the same id. Extensions already claimed by an earlier profile are filtered out, and a profile left with no extensions is dropped entirely, so each extension maps to exactly one profile.

sections.title: profileForFile
sections.explanation: Selects a profile by the lowercased file extension. Because `profiles()` already guaranteed unique extension ownership, `find` returns an unambiguous match or the function throws `UnsupportedLanguageError`.

src/languages/run.ts.overview: Runs a Language Profile's commands inside the sandbox: the toolchain preflight check and the actual test run for a Workout. It bridges the language layer (tour step 5) and the sandbox (tour step 6), turning raw process output into a normalized `TestRun` via the parsers.

sections.title: Imports and ToolchainMissingError
sections.explanation: Pulls together config (cache dir), sandbox policy and limits, the sandbox interface and the parser table. `ToolchainMissingError` includes the failing preflight command and its output so the user can see why, for example, `go` or `python3` was not found.

sections.title: preflight
sections.explanation: Runs `preflightCmd` in a throwaway temp directory inside the sandbox, with a longer 60 s timeout because a cold toolchain cache may take a while to fill. If the profile has `warmup` files they are written first (merged with support files), so tools like Go compile their test runner now rather than during the first real, time-limited run. The temp directory is always removed in `finally`.

sections.title: runTests
sections.explanation: Runs a Workout's tests once and normalizes the result. A stale result file is deleted first so old results can't be mistaken for new ones. If the sandbox stopped the run, it returns `ran: false` with a human-readable reason from `describeStop`, using the profile's limits merged over the defaults. Otherwise the matching parser from `PARSERS` reads stdout, stderr or the result file; a parser returning `undefined` means the tests never ran.

sections.title: runRequest builder
sections.explanation: Translates a profile into a sandbox `RunRequest`. Each variable in `cacheDirs` gets a persistent directory under the user cache, keyed by profile id, which is added to the env and to the writable paths. Note that `command` is always the profile's `testCmd`, never model output, matching the sandbox's contract.

src/languages/parsers.ts.overview: Parses the output of each supported test runner into Fiu's normalized `TestResult` list. Every parser returns `undefined` when the tests never got to run, which lets `runTests` distinguish a broken build from failing tests. These parsers are what make the Verified Gate language-neutral, as tour step 5 explains.

sections.title: Parser table
sections.explanation: `ParsedTests` uses `undefined` as the 'never ran' signal. `PARSERS` is a `Record<ResultFormat, ...>`, so adding a new format to the union forces a parser to be registered. TAP and JUnit prefer the result file when the profile declares one, Go reads stdout and unittest reads stderr.

sections.title: TAP parser
sections.explanation: Handles node's TAP 13 output. `# Subtest:` lines maintain a name path by indentation depth (four spaces per level), so leaf tests are named like `add > handles zero`. Suites and SKIP/TODO results are dropped. A YAML block with an `exitCode` signals a file that failed to load, so the whole run is reported as not run. `ERR_ASSERTION` distinguishes assertion failures from other errors.

sections.title: YAML block and message helpers
sections.explanation: `yamlBlock` is a minimal reader for the `---`...`...` diagnostics node attaches to TAP results: it reads top-level keys at the expected indent and supports single-line and `|`/`|-` block scalars, which is how node writes multi-line error messages. `withMessage` attaches a trimmed message only to non-passing tests.

sections.title: Go JSON parser
sections.explanation: Reads `go test -json` events line by line, ignoring non-JSON lines. It records pass/fail per test, flags tests whose output contains a panic, and collects output while skipping the runner's own `=== RUN`/`--- PASS` bookkeeping. Only leaf tests are kept (a name with a `name/child` descendant is a parent). Because Go has no assertion library, `t.Error`/`t.Fatal` failures count as assertion failures and panics as errors.

sections.title: unittest verbose parser
sections.explanation: Parses `python -m unittest -v` from stderr. A missing `Ran N tests` line or a `_FailedTest` loader entry means the run crashed. Verbose progress lines only supply names because they are fragile, while outcomes come from the `FAIL:`/`ERROR:` report blocks; an error outranks a failure when subTests report the same test several times. Skipped tests are removed and tests are named `Class.method`.

sections.title: Python traceback trimming
sections.explanation: `trimPythonTraceback` shortens a traceback to the frames in the Workout's own files, shown by base name, and strips the `^^^^` caret markers. Frames from the standard library or site-packages are hidden, but if every frame of a traceback is library code the innermost one is kept so the error still has a location. This keeps failure messages readable for both learners and LLM retry feedback.

sections.title: JUnit XML parser
sections.explanation: A regex-based JUnit reader, avoiding an XML dependency. Each `<testcase>` becomes a test named `classname.name`; `<failure>` maps to assertion-failure, `<error>` to error, and `<skipped>` cases are omitted. Messages combine the `message` attribute and the element body with CDATA unwrapped, and `decodeXml` handles numeric and named entities.

src/sandbox/sandbox.ts.overview: The sandbox front door: it defines the `Sandbox` interface every test run goes through and opens the OS-level sandbox via `@anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime`. Each run gets a fresh scratch HOME and TMPDIR, a scrubbed environment, a filesystem policy and resource limits. Tour step 6 centers on this file because Workout code is untrusted model output.

sections.title: RunRequest, Sandbox and RunResult
sections.explanation: `RunRequest` describes one command run; its doc comment states the key invariant that the command comes from a Language Profile, never from model output. Optional fields let callers add env vars, writable or readable paths, extra denied paths, a timeout and limit adjustments that can raise or lower but never disable the defaults. The `Sandbox` interface exposes `isolated` so callers know whether real isolation is in effect.

sections.title: SandboxUnavailableError and install hints
sections.explanation: Raised when no working sandbox exists. The message lists each reason and adds a platform-specific hint: the Linux packages to install (bubblewrap, socat, ripgrep), the macOS dependency, or a note that Windows needs WSL. It always mentions `--no-sandbox` as the explicit, one-off escape hatch.

sections.title: ProcessSandbox.run
sections.explanation: The single implementation behind both isolated and unisolated sandboxes, parameterized by a `wrap` function. Each run creates a temp scratch dir with `home` and `tmp`, builds the filesystem policy with the Workout dir and scratch dirs writable, and wraps the command. Because the sandbox runtime forces its own TMPDIR, the inner command re-exports TMPDIR to the run's scratch dir. It then calls `runProcess` with the scrubbed env, timeout and merged limits, and removes the scratch dir in `finally`.

sections.title: openSandbox and openUnsandboxed
sections.explanation: `openSandbox` tries the OS sandbox and only falls back to an unisolated one when the failure is a `SandboxUnavailableError` and the user passed `--no-sandbox` (`allowUnsandboxed`, never persisted). The unisolated variant uses an identity wrap, so it still gets the scrubbed env, scratch HOME, timeout and resource limits, which also makes it useful in tests.

sections.title: openOsSandbox
sections.explanation: Rejects platforms other than Linux and macOS, then lazily imports the sandbox runtime because it is large and most commands never run Workout code. It checks platform support and dependencies, then initializes the runtime with an empty, strict network allowlist, meaning no network at all. Any startup failure becomes a `SandboxUnavailableError`. The returned sandbox wraps each command with `wrapWithSandbox`, passing the per-run filesystem policy and a random command id, and resets the manager on dispose.

src/sandbox/policy.ts.overview: Pure functions that decide what Workout code may see: the filesystem policy (which paths are readable or writable) and the scrubbed environment. Keeping these as data-producing functions separates policy from enforcement, which sandbox.ts and the OS runtime handle. Tour step 6 describes how this policy denies secrets and the repository itself.

sections.title: Defaults and secret paths
sections.explanation: `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS` sets the 10 s limit for a test run. `SECRET_HOME_PATHS` lists credential locations under the user's real home (SSH keys, AWS config, `.config`, GnuPG, `.netrc`) that Workout code must never read. The canary reuses this list to prove the denial works.

sections.title: Policy types
sections.explanation: `FilesystemPolicy` has the four lists the sandbox runtime understands. `PolicyContext` carries the real home directory and the repo root, and `PolicyPaths` lists per-run writable directories plus optional extra readable and denied paths.

sections.title: filesystemPolicy
sections.explanation: Reads are allowed by default except for secret paths, the repository being drilled and any extra denied paths. The repo is denied because Workouts never need it and it may contain `.env` files or credentials. Writable paths are also added to `allowRead`, and since `allowRead` wins over a broader deny, a Workout directory that lives inside the repo stays usable. Writes are allowed only to the listed directories.

sections.title: scrubbedEnv
sections.explanation: Builds the environment from scratch instead of filtering `process.env`: only PATH and LANG are copied (with fallbacks), HOME and TMPDIR point at the run's scratch dirs, and the profile's extra variables are added. This allowlist approach guarantees that API keys and tokens in the parent environment never reach Workout code.

src/sandbox/process.ts.overview: Low-level process execution with resource limits. It runs a shell command in its own process group, enforces per-process limits through `ulimit` and whole-tree limits through a polling watchdog, and kills everything on timeout or limit breach. sandbox.ts calls it for every run, as covered in tour step 6.

sections.title: Result and limit types
sections.explanation: `ProcessResult` carries exit code, captured output and an optional `stopped` reason. `ResourceLimits` documents the two enforcement mechanisms: kernel rlimits for per-process memory and the process count, and a watchdog for summed memory and process count across the tree. Defaults are 1 GiB per process, 2 GiB total and 256 processes. `shellQuote` safely single-quotes values for the shell.

sections.title: runProcess
sections.explanation: Prefixes the command with ulimit settings and spawns it via bash (dash's `ulimit` lacks a process-count option) as a detached process group so the whole group can be killed with a negative pid. A timer stops the run on timeout, and a 250 ms watchdog walks the process tree to enforce total memory and process limits, also killing pids that escaped the group with `setsid`. On close, any background leftovers are reaped and the result records the first stop reason.

sections.title: describeStop
sections.explanation: Turns a stop reason into a readable message with a hint about the likely cause, such as an infinite loop or runaway forking. It is used both for the learner and as feedback for LLM retries; `formatMiB` prints whole GiB values nicely.

sections.title: processTree
sections.explanation: Runs `ps -A -o pid=,ppid=,rss=`, which works the same on Linux and macOS, builds a parent-to-children map, and does a breadth-first walk from the root pid to collect every descendant with its resident memory. The watchdog sums these values each tick.

sections.title: rlimitPrefix and userTaskCount
sections.explanation: Builds the `ulimit` prefix, setting both soft and hard limits so the command cannot raise them, and exits with 125 if setting them fails. The process-count limit is a fork-bomb backstop: since the kernel counts all of the user's tasks, it is set to the current task count plus 2048 headroom, capped at the existing hard limit. `userTaskCount` counts threads on Linux with `ps -L`, falling back to processes on macOS.

sections.title: Output capture
sections.explanation: Collects stream chunks up to 1 MiB and silently drops the rest, protecting Fiu from tests that print unbounded output.

src/sandbox/canary.ts.overview: Proves the sandbox actually works before Fiu trusts it. The canary runs a probe script inside the sandbox that attempts network access, writes outside the Workout, secret reads and env leakage, then checks resource limits with a memory hog and a fork loop. Results are cached for a week. Tour step 6 presents this as the verification behind the sandbox's guarantees.

sections.title: Constants and probe script
sections.explanation: `CANARY_SCRIPT` is an ES module written to disk and run inside the sandbox. It tries to open a TCP connection to 1.1.1.1:443, write inside and outside the working directory, and read each given secret path, and it reports the environment variable names. It prints one JSON line of results. Every probe except `writeInside` is expected to be refused.

sections.title: Report types
sections.explanation: `CanaryReport` is the public pass/fail result with readable failure reasons, and `CanaryOutput` mirrors the JSON the probe script prints.

sections.title: runCanary
sections.explanation: Sets up a work dir and an outside dir, plants a known secret file so the read denial is proven even on machines without `~/.ssh`, and sets a sentinel env var that must not leak. It runs the probe through the sandbox with the planted secret on the deny list, then checks each outcome and adds the resource-limit probe results. The `finally` block restores the original env var value and removes the temp directories.

sections.title: Finding real secret files
sections.explanation: Probes real files rather than directories, because the Linux sandbox hides a denied directory behind an empty mount, so listing it would succeed while showing nothing. `findFile` searches up to two levels deep in each secret location and ignores unreadable or vanished paths.

sections.title: probeResourceLimits
sections.explanation: Runs two cheap probes under deliberately low limits: four processes that together allocate about 600 MiB against a 256 MiB total, and a loop starting 100 sleeps against a limit of 32 processes. Each probe must be stopped for exactly the right reason (`memory` or `processes`), not by timeout.

sections.title: verifySandbox with cache
sections.explanation: Skips the check for unisolated sandboxes. Otherwise it reuses a cached pass if the cache key matches and the pass is less than a week old, unless `fresh` is set (as `fiu init` does). A failure throws `SandboxUnavailableError` with the canary's reasons. The cache key combines platform, CPU architecture, Node version and the installed sandbox-runtime version, so an upgrade of any of them triggers a re-check.

sections.title: Output parsing helpers
sections.explanation: `parseOutput` takes only the last stdout line as JSON so any earlier noise is ignored, returning `undefined` if the canary never produced valid output. `fail` is a small constructor for failing reports.

src/commands/drill.ts.overview: The command behind `fiu drill`, `fiu kata`, `fiu predict` and `fiu diagnose`. It turns a user-supplied target (a file, `file#symbol`, a directory, or nothing) into a fully resolved generation request: it loads config, resolves the API key, opens and verifies the sandbox, asks for consent, and then hands off to `generateWorkout`. It is the first stop of tour step 7, 'Generating a Workout', and is the orchestration layer that wires together workspace, config, consent, sandbox and synthesis.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: The import list is effectively a map of everything a generation touches: config and consent, credentials, language profiles and preflight, the sandbox and its canary check, the model factory, the Atlas search and shortlist (used to pick a target when none is given), and the workspace helpers. Note that `createModel` is imported under an alias so it can be overridden through dependency injection below.

sections.title: Options, UI and dependencies
sections.explanation: `DrillCommandOptions` mirrors CLI flags (`--yes`, `--no-sandbox`, `--quick`, `--questions`, `--what-if`) and also selects the Workout kind. `DrillUi` abstracts all user interaction (`step`, `warn`, optional `confirm`) so the CLI can render it and tests can record it; `confirm` is undefined when there is no terminal. `DrillDependencies` lets tests swap the model factory, environment and cache root. `DrillTargetError` marks user-facing target problems.

sections.title: drill: resolve config and target
sections.explanation: The command finds the repo root, makes sure the `.fiu` workspace exists and is git-excluded, and merges repo and user config. For answers-only kinds (Prediction, Diagnosis) a directory or missing target is allowed: the file is then chosen either by Atlas search for a What-if sentence or by `pickUnpractised`. The API key is resolved before anything slow happens, and a `MissingApiKeyError` is enriched with a hint to use agent mode (`/fiu-drill`) instead.

sections.title: drill: sandbox, consent, generate
sections.explanation: The sandbox is opened (or explicitly not isolated with `--no-sandbox`, which triggers a warning), checked by the canary and the language preflight, and always disposed in `finally`. Consent to send code to the provider is asked once per repository and recorded in the repo config; without a terminal and without `--yes` it fails with `ConsentRequiredError`. Finally `generateWorkout` receives the target source, its git revision, and kind-specific shaping: `quick` only applies to Drills and Katas, and Series questions only to non-What-if Predictions.

sections.title: closestTo: What-if target search
sections.explanation: When a What-if sentence is given without a file, the Atlas search finds the closest match within the requested directory. Nothing is spent until the user confirms the match; with `--yes` it is accepted directly, and without a terminal the command fails with a message telling the user the exact command to rerun.

sections.title: directoryTarget and pickUnpractised
sections.explanation: `directoryTarget` returns a repository-relative directory (empty string for the root) or `undefined` when the target is a file, refusing paths outside the repo or inside `.fiu`. `pickUnpractised` serves people who don't know file names: it takes the shortlist of dense source files and returns the first one never practised, with distinct errors for an empty shortlist and for everything already practised.

sections.title: Target parsing helpers
sections.explanation: `parseTarget` splits `path#symbol` on the last `#`, but takes the whole string literally if a file with that exact name exists, so paths containing `#` still work. An empty symbol after `#` is rejected. `repoRelative` normalises to forward-slash paths and refuses targets outside the repository or inside the `.fiu` workspace, so Fiu never drills its own Workouts.

src/synthesis/generate.ts.overview: Fiu's shared generation pipeline, used by both `fiu drill` and background refill. It calls the synthesizer, turns its outcome into a `GenerationResult`, saves verified Workouts to disk, and records every paid model call in the spend ledger whatever the outcome. It is the bridge in tour step 7 between the command layer and the synthesize/verify loop, and also handles the special case of a Prediction Series.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Pulls in cost estimation, the workout save and spend-ledger helpers, and the synthesis entry points with their attempt limits (`MAX_ATTEMPTS`, `SERIES_ATTEMPTS`). Most imports are type-only, which keeps this module a thin coordinator.

sections.title: Result and options types
sections.explanation: `GenerationResult` is a discriminated union with three outcomes: `saved` (with record, directory, test command, attempts and cost, plus an optional Series), `not-worth-practicing`, and `failed`; every branch carries a `cost`. `GenerateOptions` collects everything a generation needs, including provenance (`origin`, `commit`, `track`), Series size, and a reduced `maxAttempts` for when a daily limit has fewer attempts left.

sections.title: generateWorkout
sections.explanation: Reports the recent average spend, builds the model, and dispatches to `generateSeries` for multi-question Predictions that are neither commit-based nor What-ifs. Otherwise it runs `synthesizeDrill`, collecting `usage` events separately from progress events, then saves the verified output with `saveDrill`. The `spend` object is mutated as the outcome becomes known, and the `finally` block writes it to the ledger whenever any usage was recorded, so money spent on a failed or crashed generation is never lost.

sections.title: generateSeries
sections.explanation: Runs `synthesizeSeries` with at most `SERIES_ATTEMPTS`, then allocates one Series id and saves each verified question as its own Workout with a `series` placement (index and total). The Series' cost is split evenly across questions, with per-question `usage` cleared so totals are not double-counted. The first record is returned as the primary result, and the ledger entry lists every saved question id.

sections.title: describeEvent
sections.explanation: Turns non-usage synthesis events into the progress lines the user sees, such as 'Generating the Drill (attempt 1 of 3)' or the verifier's retry feedback. The `Exclude` type guarantees `usage` events never reach it, so the switch is exhaustive.

src/synthesis/synthesize.ts.overview: The generate-verify-retry loop at the heart of Fiu. `synthesizeDrill` asks the model for a structured Workout, checks it against the schema rules and the Verified gate, and feeds any failure back into the same conversation for up to two retries. `synthesizeSeries` does the same for a Prediction Series, keeping questions that pass and asking only for replacements. This is the core of tour step 7 and hands off to the gate covered in step 8.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Uses the Vercel AI SDK (`generateText`, `Output`, `NoObjectGeneratedError`) for structured output, the gate's `verify` and `describeFailures`, the prompt builders, and the schema module's per-kind schemas and post-hoc checks.

sections.title: Events, options and results
sections.explanation: `MAX_ATTEMPTS` is 3: one generation plus two retries, per the spec. `SynthesisEvent` includes a dedicated `usage` event emitted right after each model call, so cost is known even if a later step throws. `SynthesisResult` only offers `verified` with a verification proof, so nothing can be returned as verified without passing the gate. `SourceTooLargeError` refuses files over `MAX_SOURCE_LINES` instead of silently truncating.

sections.title: synthesizeDrill setup
sections.explanation: Validates the source size (and the pre-commit source for commit Predictions), and derives the `fromCommit` and `whatIf` flags that select different prompts and schemas. The conversation starts with a single user message and only ever grows, so each retry sees its own earlier attempts and the feedback on them.

sections.title: synthesizeDrill attempt loop
sections.explanation: Each attempt generates with a kind-specific system prompt and schema, appends the model's response to the conversation, and short-circuits on `worthPracticing: false`. Schema failures and `checkWorkoutOutput` problems become `[schema]` feedback; otherwise the candidate goes through `verify` in the sandbox. For a What-if, the source itself is the 'before' and the reference solution is the 'after'. Failures are described and appended as a retry prompt; after the last attempt the result is `failed` with the final feedback.

sections.title: Series types
sections.explanation: A Series gets only two attempts (`SERIES_ATTEMPTS`): the first call and one retry for the questions that failed. Each kept question records the attempt that produced it.

sections.title: synthesizeSeries
sections.explanation: One call returns a shared reference solution plus several questions; `expandSeries` turns each into a standalone Prediction. Each question is schema-checked, checked for overlaps with earlier and already-kept questions, and verified on its own, and only those that pass are kept. A retry asks only for the missing number of replacements. Partial success counts: if any question was kept the result is `verified`, and a later 'not worth practicing' answer simply stops the loop.

sections.title: generate: one model call
sections.explanation: Wraps `generateText` with structured output and a 32k output-token cap. The per-kind schema is cast to `AnyWorkoutOutputSchema` because every kind's schema is a subset of it. Only `NoObjectGeneratedError` is caught: a malformed object is worth a retry, and its raw text is kept in the conversation so the model can see its mistake, while auth, network or quota errors propagate. Usage is extracted even from the error, because malformed answers are still billed.

src/synthesis/model.ts.overview: A small factory that turns a configured provider, model id and API key into an AI SDK `LanguageModel` plus provider-specific request options. It supports Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, and is the injectable dependency that `drill.ts` and `generate.ts` use in tour step 7.

sections.title: Types and capability check
sections.explanation: `ProviderOptions` is derived from the AI SDK's own `generateText` parameter type rather than redeclared, so it stays in sync with the library. `ModelChoice` pairs a model with its options. `SUPPORTS_ADAPTIVE_FALLBACKS` is a regex over model ids that gates the newer Anthropic-only settings.

sections.title: createModel
sections.explanation: A switch over the provider builds the matching SDK client with the user's key. For recent Claude models it enables adaptive thinking, high effort and API-chosen fallbacks on refusal, because Workout design is intelligence-sensitive coding work. Older configured models might reject those settings, so they get empty options, as do OpenAI and Google.

src/synthesis/prompt.ts.overview: All the text Fiu sends to the model: one system prompt per Workout kind (Drill, Kata, Prediction, Diagnosis), Series add-ons, the user prompt that presents the numbered source file, and retry prompts that carry verifier feedback. The prompts encode the product rules (one small bug, faithful reference solution, plain-English options) that the schema checks and the Verified gate later enforce. It is part of tour step 7.

sections.title: DrillTarget and size limit
sections.explanation: `DrillTarget` describes what the model works from: the repo-relative path and source, an optional pinned symbol, an optional commit change (with diff and, for Predictions, the file before it), an optional What-if sentence, and an optional Track placement. `MAX_SOURCE_LINES` (3000) is the cap beyond which the user should pin a symbol in a smaller file instead of having the source truncated silently.

sections.title: Drill system prompt
sections.explanation: Describes a Drill as a 3 AM incident: extract one unit, make it self-contained with inline fakes, inject exactly one realistic bug in at most 3 lines from a listed set of bug families, and write 3 to 5 tests where the bug fails by assertion rather than crashing. It spells out spoiler rules for hints, the README and source anchors. Language-specific rules come from the profile's `promptRules`, and a Quick variant adds size limits from `QUICK`.

sections.title: Kata system prompt
sections.explanation: A Kata removes one contiguous region (5-25 lines, or 5-12 when Quick) and replaces it with a compiling placeholder that returns a wrong but type-correct value, never a throw. The README is a contract brief, and hints may name the approach but never the code. `gapSummary` is an internal note that is never shown.

sections.title: Prediction system prompt
sections.explanation: For people who don't read code: a plain-English Scenario with four options, each wrong option backed by a small Variant of the reference solution and a test that proves its outcome. Extra rule blocks are appended for a What-if (the reference solution has the change, `previous` is today's code) and for a Prediction from a commit (`previous` is the pre-commit code and must not be mentioned). These rules mirror the `previous` checks in the gate.

sections.title: Diagnosis system prompt
sections.explanation: A Diagnosis presents a practice incident and four Causes, each a Variant with a Symptom test. Unlike a Prediction, the reference solution is the healthy code, so every Symptom test must fail against it. The prompt puts a lot of weight on making wrong Causes plausible, so that choosing requires a real picture of the system rather than word matching with the incident.

sections.title: Series rules and retry
sections.explanation: `seriesRules` is appended to the Prediction prompt: one shared extraction, then several questions that must each ask about a different rule, with no shared Scenario, correct outcome or Variant. `seriesRetryPrompt` tells the model how many questions were saved and asks for replacements of the discarded ones only.

sections.title: systemPromptFor dispatcher
sections.explanation: A single expression that selects the system prompt for a kind and forwards the `quick`, `fromCommit` and `whatIf` options to the builders that use them.

sections.title: drillUserPrompt
sections.explanation: Builds the user message: the source with right-aligned line numbers (so the model can produce accurate source anchors), a focus sentence chosen by priority (What-if without a symbol, pinned symbol, commit with before-file, commit only, or a default by kind), and optional `<diff>`, `<source-before-commit>` and Track context. XML-like tags separate the source from the instructions.

sections.title: retryPrompt
sections.explanation: The message appended after a failed attempt: it says the Workout was discarded, includes the verifier's feedback verbatim, and asks for a corrected version that fixes every problem listed.

src/synthesis/schema.ts.overview: The Zod schemas that define each Workout kind's structured output, plus the post-hoc checks the schemas cannot express. The schemas deliberately stick to types, enums and descriptions, because provider support for numeric, length and pattern constraints varies; `checkWorkoutOutput` enforces those rules afterwards and returns human-readable problems used as retry feedback. It is the first file of tour step 8, 'Schemas and the Verified Gate'.

sections.title: Kinds and shared constants
sections.explanation: Defines the four `WorkoutKind`s, their display `NOUN`s, and `answersOnly` for the two kinds aimed at people who don't read code (Prediction and Diagnosis). `SECRET` names what each kind's source anchors must stay silent about, and is interpolated into schema descriptions.

sections.title: Field builders
sections.explanation: `baseFields`, `codeFields` and `solutionFields` are functions of the kind, so the same field gets kind-specific `.describe()` text, and those descriptions act as inline instructions to the model. `OriginalDefectSchema` is always present and uses zeros or empty strings for 'none', because optional fields are unreliable in structured output across providers.

sections.title: Drill, Kata and Prediction schemas
sections.explanation: Each kind's schema is composed by spreading field builders. Predictions have four options, each with a `variant` (an `original` snippet to replace and its `changed` text) and a `misunderstanding`. `CommitPredictionOutputSchema` and `WhatIfOutputSchema` extend it with `previous` code and a `previous` flag on options; the What-if also adds `modelledAs` and caps the change at `WHAT_IF_MAX_CHANGED_LINES` (10).

sections.title: Diagnosis schema
sections.explanation: A Diagnosis has four Causes, each with text, a Symptom, a test name and a Variant; unlike Prediction options, the true Cause has a Variant too, because the reference solution is the healthy code.

sections.title: Series schema and overlap check
sections.explanation: `PredictionSeriesOutputSchema` shares one unit, reference solution and anchors across several `SeriesQuestionSchema`s, reusing field definitions through `.shape`. `expandSeries` merges the shared fields into each question to produce standalone Predictions. `seriesOverlaps` compares normalised scenarios, true outcomes and Variants against earlier and already-saved questions, and returns problems keyed by question index.

sections.title: AnyWorkoutOutput and schema selection
sections.explanation: `AnyWorkoutOutputSchema` is the union-of-fields shape with kind-specific fields optional. Agent mode's `submit_drill` accepts it, and `synthesize.ts` casts every per-kind schema to it. `outputSchemaFor` picks the right schema from the kind and the `fromCommit` and `whatIf` flags.

sections.title: checkWorkoutOutput
sections.explanation: Enforces the rules the schemas cannot express: kebab-case slug, minute ranges (answers-only kinds are always Quick), valid anchor ranges, spoiler words in Drill anchors and READMEs, exactly two hints, Quick size limits, and comments on the bug lines that point at the bug (through `bugComments`). It then delegates to `predictionProblems`, `diagnosisProblems` or `kataLeaks` as appropriate.

sections.title: Prediction problems and code vocabulary
sections.explanation: `codeVocabulary` extracts identifiers that look like code (camelCase, inner capitals, snake_case, at least 4 characters). `predictionProblems` validates the `previous` option rules for each mode, exactly four options with one correct, unique test names, that each wrong option's `variant.original` occurs exactly once, and that no user-facing text leaks code names.

sections.title: Diagnosis problems and Kata leaks
sections.explanation: `diagnosisProblems` mirrors the Prediction checks for Causes, and also requires distinct Symptoms and a Variant on every Cause. `kataLeaks` diffs the reference solution against the starting code and flags any removed line of 15 or more characters that appears verbatim in the brief or hints. `checkDrillOutput` is a kept-for-compatibility wrapper.

src/verify/gate.ts.overview: The Verified gate: the guarantee that no Workout is saved unless its tests prove it behaves as claimed. It writes candidate code and tests to fresh temp directories, runs them in the sandbox, and applies kind-specific checks. Drills and Katas need a passing reference and a failing starting code; Predictions and Diagnoses need each option or Cause to be pinned by exactly one test across all Variants. It runs every check rather than stopping at the first failure, so the retry prompt can report everything at once. It is the centrepiece of tour step 8.

sections.title: Candidate and result types
sections.explanation: `Candidate` is the subset of a generated Workout the gate needs, with kind-specific optional fields (starting code, regression test, options, causes, previous and before/after sources). `Check` enumerates every check category used in feedback tags. `Verification` either carries the proof runs or a list of `CheckFailure`s. The size constants encode the product rules: a Drill changes at most 3 lines, and a Kata's gap removes 5-25 lines (5-12 when Quick) with at most 3 placeholder lines.

sections.title: verify and temp runs
sections.explanation: `verify` dispatches Predictions and Diagnoses to their own gates. For Drills and Katas it runs the tests against both the reference solution and the starting code, then concatenates every check's failures. `runInTempWorkout` writes the profile's support files, code and tests into a fresh `mkdtemp` directory, runs them in the sandbox, and always removes the directory.

sections.title: Drill and Kata checks
sections.explanation: The reference must pass every test. The starting code must run, have at least one assertion failure and at least one pass, and no crashes, since a crash would make the Workout look simply broken. A Drill's regression test must exist uniquely and fail by assertion; `findTests` matches exact names or trailing path segments such as `add > wrong`. `checkMinimalDiff` requires exactly one diff hunk and enforces the Drill and Kata size limits.

sections.title: Prediction gate
sections.explanation: `buildVariant` applies a snippet replacement, using a replacer function so `$` patterns in the changed text are not interpreted. Each wrong option's code is its Variant, or the Previous Version for the old-behaviour option. The gate runs the reference and every wrong version, then checks test ownership, that only the expected option's test passes for each version, and either `checkPrevious` or `checkVariantDiff`.

sections.title: Diagnosis gate
sections.explanation: Every Cause, the true one included, is a Variant. Against the healthy reference no Symptom test may pass (`checkNoSymptom`); against each Cause's Variant only that Cause's test passes. The generic source match is turned off in `checkVariantDiff` and replaced with a Diagnosis-specific rule: a wrong Cause must not be what the source already does, while a true Cause found in the source is allowed and becomes the notice that the bug may be real.

sections.title: Option test and outcome checks
sections.explanation: `checkOptionTests` makes sure each option names exactly one existing test and that no test is left without an owner. `checkOutcomes` checks one code version: only the expected option's test may pass, the rest must fail by assertion, and crashes are always problems. A missing test is skipped here because the option-tests check already reports it.

sections.title: Previous Version and Variant diffs
sections.explanation: `checkPrevious` requires the Previous Version to differ from the reference, caps What-if changes, rejects twins of earlier Variants, and uses `unanchoredRegions` to confirm that each differing region really comes from the before-file. That check is skipped for fetched Workouts that have no source. `checkVariantDiff` requires one hunk of at most 3 lines, no duplicates, and that the Variant is not what the source itself does, because then that option would actually be the true one.

sections.title: Feedback formatting
sections.explanation: `describeFailures` renders each failure as `[check] message` followed by the test output, keeping only the last 4000 characters because the tail of a test log is usually where the failure is. Small helpers format test lists, outcome verbs and hunk locations for messages.

src/verify/defect.ts.overview: Detects and anchors defects relative to the real source file. It finds whether the original code already contains a Workout's 'injected' bug (an Original Defect, reported only after an Attempt), detects comments that give the bug away, and checks that a Prediction's Previous Version is truly anchored in the pre-commit file. Used by the schema checks, the gate, and saving, as part of tour step 8.

sections.title: OriginalDefect and line normalisation
sections.explanation: `OriginalDefect` records the source lines, a description, and the evidence behind it: a source match, the model's own report, or both. `normaliseLine` strips trailing comments and all whitespace so formatting differences don't block matches; it is deliberately naive about comment markers inside strings. `SIGNIFICANT_LINE_CHARS` (8) excludes short lines such as `}` or `return` that would match too easily to count as evidence.

sections.title: bugRegion and matchSource
sections.explanation: `bugRegion` requires exactly one diff hunk between the reference and the buggy code. `matchSource` reports where the source already contains the buggy lines: every significant buggy line must be found and no significant fixed line may be present. It returns the min-max line span, or `undefined` when the bug only removes lines.

sections.title: findOriginalDefect
sections.explanation: Combines two kinds of evidence. The model's `originalDefect` report is only trusted if it has a description and valid in-file lines, and an invalid report is silently ignored rather than costing a retry. A source match is attempted for Drills and for a Diagnosis's true Cause, whose bug is rebuilt by applying its Variant. A match wins and is labelled `both` when the model agrees; otherwise the model's report alone is used.

sections.title: bugComments
sections.explanation: Returns the comments on the buggy lines that the fixed lines don't have, since such comments would point at the bug. `checkWorkoutOutput` uses it to reject Drills whose starting code annotates its own bug.

sections.title: unanchoredRegions
sections.explanation: For each diff hunk between the reference and the Previous Version, at least one significant line must be found only in the old file. If the Previous Version side is empty (the commit added lines), a reference line found only in the new file anchors it instead. One line is enough, because extraction renames things around a change. Unanchored regions are returned with a concrete missing line, so the retry feedback can say exactly what to copy.

src/verify/diff.ts.overview: A minimal line diff based on longest common subsequence, grouped into contiguous hunks. The gate uses it to require a single small changed region, the schema checks use it to detect Kata leaks, and defect detection uses it to locate bug regions. It belongs to tour step 8.

sections.title: Hunk and normalisation
sections.explanation: A `Hunk` records the 1-based start line in the original text plus the removed and added lines. `normalisedLines` treats CRLF, trailing whitespace and trailing blank lines as non-differences, so model formatting noise doesn't create spurious hunks.

sections.title: LCS table
sections.explanation: Builds a suffix LCS table with `Uint32Array` rows: `lcs[i][j]` is the LCS length of `a[i..]` and `b[j..]`. This is O(n·m) in time and memory, which is acceptable because Workout files are small single units.

sections.title: Walking into hunks
sections.explanation: Walks both texts forward: equal lines flush the current hunk, and otherwise the table decides whether to take an added or a removed line, preferring additions on ties. Consecutive changes accumulate into one hunk anchored at the current original line, so a replaced block becomes a single hunk with both removed and added lines.

src/workouts/save.ts.overview: Defines the on-disk `WorkoutRecord` (workout.json) and writes a Verified Workout into `.fiu/workouts/<id>/`: the starting code and tests for Drills and Katas, a hidden `.solution/` with the reference solution and the original tests, and a README written by Fiu. It also records provenance (git commit and dirtiness, cost) and optional enrichments such as Original Defects and 'Around this code'. It is the first file of tour step 9, 'Storing Workouts and Attempts'.

sections.title: Provenance and placement types
sections.explanation: `SourceRevision` and `SourceAnchor` tie a Workout to the commit its anchors point into. `Generator` and `Origin` say who wrote it (Fiu or the user's agent) and why it exists (manual, agent task, commit, or a Track step). `TrackPlacement` deliberately leaves out the step number, since a dropped step would make a stored number wrong for good. `WhatIfPlacement` and `SeriesPlacement` carry the What-if sentence and the position in a Series.

sections.title: WorkoutRecord
sections.explanation: The metadata saved as `workout.json`. Optional fields are documented for backward compatibility: Workouts made before agent mode have no `generator` or `origin`. Kind-specific blocks (`prediction`, `diagnosis`, `gapSummary`, `regressionTestName`) live side by side, and `files` maps logical roles (code, test, solution, originalTest, previous) to paths inside the Workout directory.

sections.title: sourceRevision
sections.explanation: Uses `git rev-parse` to get HEAD (treating a repo with no commits as dirty with no commit) and `git status --porcelain` on the single file to tell whether it differs from that commit or is untracked.

sections.title: saveDrill
sections.explanation: Builds a unique id from kind, date and slug, works out the Original Defect when the source is available, and builds 'Around this code' through a failure-tolerant wrapper. Answers-only kinds have no code to edit, so their `code` and `test` entries point at the `.solution` files and no starting files are written. Every file, including the pretty-printed `workout.json`, is written with parent directories created as needed.

sections.title: Ids for Series and Workouts
sections.explanation: `newSeriesId` scans existing `workout.json` files for Series ids already in use, and `uniqueId` checks both `workouts/` and the legacy `done/` directory. Both add a `-2`, `-3`, ... suffix until the id is free.

sections.title: Provenance and Prediction README
sections.explanation: `provenance` explains which commit the Workout came from and what it cost, or that it was made by the user's agent and not measured. `predictionReadme` is written by Fiu rather than the model, and sorts the options alphabetically so their written order (where the correct one might be first) gives nothing away. The answer and the anchors stay in `workout.json` until after answering. `whatIfLines` shows the human's sentence next to how the model understood it.

sections.title: Diagnosis README
sections.explanation: Marks the incident clearly as a practice incident, since readers can't see the code to tell. The incident shown is the true Cause's Symptom, and the Causes are again sorted alphabetically to hide which one was written as correct.

sections.title: README helpers and Drill README
sections.explanation: `aroundLines` and `trackPlacement` add optional context at the top of every README. The Drill and Kata `readme` appends the model's incident report or brief, then source anchor links computed relative to the Workout directory with `#L` line fragments, then provenance.

sections.title: safeAround
sections.explanation: 'Around this code' is an extra: any exception while building it is swallowed and the Verified Workout is saved without it. Saving must never fail because of an optional enrichment.

src/workouts/store.ts.overview: The persistence layer for `.fiu/state.json` and the Workout directory listing.
