It defines Zod schemas for Attempt outcomes, the spend ledger, discards and background refill bookkeeping, with preprocessors that migrate older formats, and provides queries such as listing Workouts with a derived status, Series navigation, discard and restore, and average spend. Part of tour step 9.

sections.title: Outcome schema with v1 migration
sections.explanation: `OutcomeSchema` uses `z.preprocess` to rename v1's `attempts` field to `runs` on read, so old state files parse without a separate migration step. Outcomes record completion or abandonment, hints used, an optional rating, defect confirmation, and confidence for answers-only kinds. `DiscardSchema` records when and why a Workout was archived.

sections.title: Cost and spend ledger schemas
sections.explanation: `SpendSchema` records each generation request whatever its result, including non-Workout calls such as `track-plan` and `atlas`. A preprocessor maps the project's former names (`fiutsu`, `kintsugi`) to `fiu`, and the generator defaults to `fiu` for entries made before agent mode. `cost` is nullable because Fiu can't see the usage of an agent-generated Workout.

sections.title: State schema and IO
sections.explanation: `StateSchema` uses `.default()` throughout so a minimal or older `state.json` (or none at all) parses into a complete state. `readState`, `writeState` and `recordSpend` do a simple read-modify-write of the whole file, with no locking, and validate each new spend entry before appending it.

sections.title: averageSpend
sections.explanation: Averages the last N fully priced requests for Workouts, excluding Track planning, Atlas calls, agent-generated entries (null cost) and entries with unpriced models. Filtering by kind relies on Workout ids starting with `<kind>_`, a convention set by `saveDrill`.

sections.title: Errors and status types
sections.explanation: User-facing errors include the command that fixes the problem (`fiu train`, `fiu restore`). `WorkoutStatus` is derived rather than stored: queued (never attempted), in-progress (an open Attempt), attempted, or discarded.

sections.title: Listing and status derivation
sections.explanation: `listWorkouts` reads every directory's `workout.json`, skips directories without one, and sorts newest first. `statusOf` checks discards first, then Attempt records, and treats any v1 outcome as 'attempted' because v1 recorded outcomes against Workouts it later moved away. `loadWorkout` finds a Workout by id through the full listing.

sections.title: Discard, Series and restore
sections.explanation: Discarding archives a Workout in state without deleting files, so it can be restored. Series helpers order questions by index, and `nextInSeries` prefers the next unanswered question after the current one, falling back to an earlier open one. `discardSeries` discards only questions nobody has answered yet.

sections.title: Outcomes and legacy notice
sections.explanation: `recordOutcome` validates and appends a finished Attempt's outcome. `legacyDoneNotice` tells users that Workouts finished under v1 stay in `done/` and are not listed, because their starting code was edited in place and they can't be redone.

src/workouts/attempts.ts.overview: Manages Attempts: each try at a Workout gets its own numbered directory under the attempts folder, holding a fresh copy of the Starting Code and an `attempt.json` record of progress and outcome. The Workout itself is never edited, so retries always start from the Verified original. This is the persistence layer the training session (Step 10) builds on, and it is part of Step 9's storage story.

sections.title: Imports and record file name
sections.explanation: Pulls in filesystem helpers plus the `LanguageProfile`, `WorkspacePaths` and `WorkoutRecord` types. `ATTEMPT_FILE` names the single bookkeeping file kept inside each Attempt directory, next to the human's working copy.

sections.title: AttemptRecord and Confidence types
sections.explanation: `AttemptRecord` captures everything about one try: counters for save-triggered runs and Hints, timestamps, outcome, rating, and whether the human confirmed a reported source defect. Prediction and Diagnosis Attempts add `order` (the per-Attempt shuffle), `answer` and `confidence`. `Attempt` pairs the record with the directory where the human works.

sections.title: Listing Attempt records
sections.explanation: `listAttemptRecords` reads every `attempt.json` under the Workout's attempts folder and returns them sorted by number. A missing folder simply means no Attempts yet, so it returns an empty array instead of throwing.

sections.title: Opening or resuming an Attempt
sections.explanation: `openAttempt` enforces one open Attempt per Workout: if a record without an outcome exists it is resumed. Otherwise it allocates the next number and copies support files, code and test from the Workout directory. Prediction and Diagnosis Workouts have no code to edit, so nothing is copied; instead the options or Causes get a shuffled display order so a retry cannot be answered by remembering a position. `now` and `random` are injectable for deterministic tests.

sections.title: Fisher-Yates shuffle
sections.explanation: A standard Fisher-Yates shuffle of indices `0..n-1`, driven by the injected `random` function. Storing indices rather than shuffled options keeps the Workout's own option list canonical.

sections.title: Saving and path helpers
sections.explanation: `saveAttempt` rewrites `attempt.json` so a resumed Attempt keeps its counts. `attemptDir` centralizes the `<attemptsDir>/<workoutId>/<number>` layout, and `isAttemptBookkeeping` lets the file watcher ignore the record file so writing progress never triggers a test run.

src/workouts/queue.ts.overview: Decides which Workout `fiu quick` should serve next. It defines what counts as a Quick Workout by measuring the Workout itself, then ranks queued candidates by preferred kind, by whether they came from AI-written code, and by recency. It sits between the Workout store (Step 9) and the `quick` entry points in commands/train.ts (Step 10).

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Uses the `QUICK` limits and `answersOnly` helper from the synthesis schema, plus `listWorkouts` from the store, which returns Workouts newest first.

sections.title: Deciding whether a Workout is Quick
sections.explanation: `isQuick` checks the Workout's own numbers rather than how it was requested: estimated minutes must be within `QUICK.maxMinutes`. Answer-only kinds (Prediction, Diagnosis) show no code, so minutes alone decide; otherwise the Starting Code file must be short enough. A missing code file makes it not Quick.

sections.title: Preferring AI-written code
sections.explanation: `fromAiCode` flags Workouts generated from an agent task or from a commit marked as AI-co-authored. The comment states the rationale: practising code an AI wrote is what pays down comprehension debt.

sections.title: Picking the next Quick Workout
sections.explanation: `nextQuickWorkout` filters to queued Workouts that are not Track steps (origin `explore`), whose source file still exists, and that are Quick. It then sorts by the index of the kind in the preferred `kinds` list (unlisted kinds last), then AI-written first. Because `listWorkouts` is newest first and `Array.prototype.sort` is stable, ties keep the newest Workout on top without an explicit date comparison.

src/commands/train.ts.overview: Implements `fiu train`, `fiu quick` and `fiu quick --while`. It selects a Workout, opens an Attempt, and then drives one of three interaction loops: a save-triggered test loop for Drills and Katas, or a single-answer reveal for Predictions (including What-ifs) and Diagnoses. All terminal I/O goes through the injected `TrainIo` interface, while the actual logic lives in `TrainingSession`; this is the orchestration layer described in Step 10.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Brings together nearly every subsystem: config, background refill expiry, cost description, the background-command runner, watcher, renderer and session, the sandbox and its canary, language preflight, Attempts, the queue, the Debrief, and the Workout store.

sections.title: IO, options and result types
sections.explanation: `TrainIo` abstracts the terminal: printing, reading a key (abortable), picking among Workouts, rating, confirming a defect, and optional editor and spinner hooks. Abstracting this lets tests drive a whole session without a TTY. `TrainDependencies` injects config env, cache root, watcher debounce and the optional background command; `TrainResult` enumerates how a session can end.

sections.title: fiu quick
sections.explanation: `quick` first expires stale commit Workouts (which also frees queue slots), then asks the queue for the best Quick Workout using the repository's preferred kinds (falling back to the user's), and delegates to `train` with its id. `KEYS_HELP` is the key legend shown after each run.

sections.title: train: selecting a Workout
sections.explanation: With an explicit id any non-discarded Workout can be redone. Without one, in-progress Workouts are listed before queued ones, and each Series collapses into a single row: its open question, or else its lowest-index unanswered question. A single choice is taken directly; otherwise the user picks.

sections.title: train: dispatching by kind
sections.explanation: Resolves config and the Language Profile, then branches. Diagnoses and Predictions run without any sandbox, since their outcomes were measured at Verification time; Predictions loop to offer the next Series question on `[n]`. Drills and Katas open a sandbox, verify it with the canary, run the toolchain preflight, open the Attempt and enter `runSession`, disposing the sandbox in a `finally`.

sections.title: runSession: the save-and-run loop
sections.explanation: Prints the header with file paths, warns if the source changed, and opens the editor. Test runs are serialized: a save during a run sets `rerun` so exactly one more run follows. The watcher triggers runs on content changes, a background command's completion is announced with a bell, and `Promise.race` between the finished promise and the key reader decides the outcome. The in-flight run is awaited before closing, and quitting leaves the Attempt open for resumption.

sections.title: Closing an Attempt and the Debrief
sections.explanation: `closeAttempt` is shared by all kinds: it shows the possible-real-bug notice (asking for confirmation only on the first finished Attempt), the Debrief, then the rating, and records the outcome via `session.finish`. `showDebrief` retries without context profiles if building fails and swallows write errors, because the Debrief is an extra that must never block closing.

sections.title: Answer flows: Diagnosis, Prediction, What-if
sections.explanation: `readAnswer` maps number keys back through the shuffled indices and then asks for confidence before the reveal, so confidence reflects the answer rather than the outcome. `runDiagnosis` and `runPrediction` print the incident or scenario, record one answer, reveal the truth, and offer `[d]` to show the code difference behind a wrong answer. Predictions from a commit explain the old behaviour as a fact; What-ifs always show both today and the changed behaviour plus `WHAT_IF_LIMITS`.

sections.title: Defect and change descriptions
sections.explanation: `describeDefect` formats the warning that the Workout's bug may exist in the real source, distinguishing model-claimed defects from matching logic, and is only shown after an Attempt so it never narrows the search. `describeChange` names the commit that changed a Prediction's behaviour and whether an AI co-wrote it.

sections.title: Key reader and fiu quick --while
sections.explanation: `readKeys` handles hint, give up (showing the solution diff), background status and quit; it returns a never-resolving promise after finishing so the race is decided by `finished`. `quickWhile` starts the user's command in the background, serves Quick Workouts back to back while it runs, and then waits for it with a `[q]` stop key. Errors in Fiu are caught and reported so a failure never costs the user their command.

src/runner/session.ts.overview: `TrainingSession` holds the logic of one sitting with one Attempt: running tests and judging verdicts, Hints, solution and variant diffs, recording answers, and finishing with an outcome. It deliberately holds no terminal state so it can be driven by tests as well as by `fiu train`. Progress is persisted to the Attempt as it happens, which is what makes resumption work (Step 10).

sections.title: Imports and verdict types
sections.explanation: `RunVerdict` distinguishes tests that did not run, failing tests, all-passing but with an edited test file, and completed. `SessionRun` bundles the raw `TestRun`, its verdict and the save-triggered run count.

sections.title: Session options
sections.explanation: The options carry the immutable Workout, the Attempt, the profile, and an optional sandbox, which is absent for Predictions and Diagnoses because nothing runs during their Attempts. `contextProfiles` is set when context is on so the Debrief can read the Atlas; `now` is injectable for tests.

sections.title: Class shell and accessors
sections.explanation: Options are stored in a private `#options` field, with read-only getters for the Workout, paths, Attempt and Hint count. A private `#finished` flag guards against finishing twice.

sections.title: Running tests and judging verdicts
sections.explanation: `runTests` increments and saves the run count only for save-triggered runs, then runs the profile's tests in the sandbox. `#verdict` treats zero tests as failing, and an all-pass run counts only if `testsEdited` finds the Attempt's test file identical to the Workout's original. That check prevents completing a Workout by weakening its tests.

sections.title: Hints and solution diff
sections.explanation: `nextHint` increments and persists `hintsUsed` before returning, so a Hint counts even across resumes. `solutionDiff` diffs the human's current code against the Reference Solution, used when giving up.

sections.title: Options, Causes and answers
sections.explanation: `predictionOptions` and `diagnosisCauses` return items in the Attempt's shuffled order, keeping the original index so the answer maps back correctly. `answer` and `diagnose` save the chosen index and return the outcome: right means completed, wrong means abandoned, with the truth returned for the reveal.

sections.title: Variant diff, source change and first finisher
sections.explanation: `variantDiff` shows what would have to change for a chosen option to be true: either the commit's previous code against the reference, or the reference against `buildVariant` of the option's variant. `sourceChanged` uses `git diff --quiet` against the anchor commit. `firstToFinish` ensures the real-defect question is asked only once per Workout.

sections.title: Finishing the Attempt
sections.explanation: `finish` writes outcome, timestamp and optional rating, defect confirmation and confidence into the Attempt record and also into state.json via `recordOutcome`. Optional answers are spread in only when present so absent fields stay absent. The Workout itself is never modified.

sections.title: Hunk formatting and watcher ignore rules
sections.explanation: `formatHunks` renders diff hunks as `@@ line N @@` blocks with `-`/`+` lines. `ignoredByWatcher` lists paths that must not trigger runs: the Attempt bookkeeping file, the profile's result file, caches like `__pycache__` and `node_modules`, Emacs lock files, and editor swap or temp files.

src/runner/watch.ts.overview: A small, careful file watcher used by `fiu train` to rerun tests on save. Rather than trusting raw filesystem events, it compares a content fingerprint of the Attempt directory and only fires once content has actually changed and settled. This filters out touches, editor temp files and half-written saves (Step 10).

sections.title: Options
sections.explanation: `WatchOptions` takes an `ignore` predicate over relative paths and an optional debounce quiet period.

sections.title: watchForChanges
sections.explanation: Takes an initial fingerprint, then on any non-ignored event debounces and calls `check`. `check` re-fingerprints repeatedly until two consecutive reads match, because saves often truncate then write. Only if the settled fingerprint differs from the last one does `onChange` fire, so touch-without-change is ignored. It uses Node's recursive `fs.watch`, and `close` stops both the timer and the watcher.

sections.title: contentFingerprint
sections.explanation: Hashes the sorted list of non-ignored files, each as path, a NUL separator, the content and another NUL, with SHA-256. Paths are normalized to forward slashes for portability. A file deleted between listing and reading is tolerated, and its missing content becomes part of the fingerprint.

src/runner/render.ts.overview: Formats a `SessionRun` as terminal text for `fiu train`: a pass count, a mark per test, truncated failure messages, and fallbacks when there is nothing to show. It is pure string formatting with no I/O, kept separate from the session logic (Step 10).

sections.title: Marks and limits
sections.explanation: Maps each test outcome to a mark (pass, assertion failure, error) and sets limits on how much runner output and per-test message text to show.

sections.title: formatRun
sections.explanation: Labels the run as the initial run or `Run N`. When tests did not run, it shows the tail of the raw output. Otherwise it lists each test with its mark and a truncated message; if a failure has no message, it falls back to the runner's own output. An edited-tests verdict gets an explicit instruction to restore the original tests.

sections.title: Text helpers
sections.explanation: `head` keeps the first lines of a message, `tail` keeps the last lines of runner output (where errors usually are), each adding an ellipsis when truncated. `indent` prefixes every line with four spaces.

src/atlas/skeleton.ts.overview: Builds the Atlas skeleton: the model-free structure of the repository that every Atlas operation starts from. It lists tracked files via git, keeps those with a known Language Profile, and records their git blob hash, line count, symbols, logic score and key functions, then derives folders with a hash of their contents' names. Hashes are what make Atlas descriptions detectably current or stale (Step 11).

sections.title: Imports and error type
sections.explanation: Uses `git` via execa, logic scoring from the explore shortlist, drillable-path rules, profile lookup, the line limit for drilling, and the symbol extractor. `AtlasTargetError` signals a bad folder argument.

sections.title: Skeleton types
sections.explanation: `SkeletonFile` records the path, git blob hash, line count, whether it is described (not test, generated or vendored), whether it is too long to drill, an optional logic score, its symbols and key function names. `SkeletonFolder` holds sorted child folders and files plus a hash over their names, so a folder is re-described when its membership changes.

sections.title: Blob hash and parent helper
sections.explanation: `blobHash` reproduces git's own blob hash (`blob <len>\0` plus content, SHA-1), so a description written on one clone matches identical content on another, working-tree changes included. `parentOf` maps top-level paths to the root `''`.

sections.title: buildSkeleton
sections.explanation: Lists tracked files with `git ls-files -z`, skips files with no supported profile and unreadable files, and builds a `SkeletonFile` for each. Folders are created lazily and recursively register themselves with their parents. Each folder's hash is computed over its sorted subfolder names (with trailing slash) and file names.

sections.title: skeletonFile
sections.explanation: Computes one file's entry from its content: lines, described flag, symbols from `extractSymbols` (with the profile's optional custom pattern), logic score and blob hash. Key functions are only computed for described files.

sections.title: Folder ordering and scope
sections.explanation: `foldersBottomUp` returns folders within a scope deepest first, the order the Atlas describes them so subfolders are ready when their parent is described. `atlasScope` turns a CLI path argument into a repository-relative folder, rejecting paths outside the repo, single files, and folders with no recognised source.

src/atlas/symbols.ts.overview: A language-neutral, regex-based symbol extractor for the Atlas. It finds declarations line by line across TypeScript/JavaScript, Python, Go, Rust and similar languages, computes each one's line range by brace matching or indentation, scores it by branch density, and picks a file's key functions. Being heuristic and dependency-free keeps the skeleton cheap to rebuild (Step 11).

sections.title: AtlasSymbol and key-function limits
sections.explanation: A symbol has a name (`Class.method` for methods), a 1-based inclusive line range, a callable flag and a score using the same branch-per-line measure as file logic scores. Key functions are callables of at least 5 lines, at most 5 per file.

sections.title: Declaration patterns
sections.explanation: `PATTERNS` are tried in order per line: Go methods with receivers, function keywords (`function`, `def`, `func`, `fn`), classes and traits as containers, Rust `impl` blocks, type-like declarations, arrow-function constants, and indented method headers. The method pattern is only kept inside a class. `NOT_A_NAME` rejects keywords like `if` or `return` that the method pattern would otherwise match on call-like lines.

sections.title: extractSymbols
sections.explanation: First collects declarations with their indentation, using the first matching pattern per line; a profile's `declarationPattern` replaces the built-ins entirely. Each declaration's end is bounded by the next declaration at the same or outer indent. Then it drops anything nested inside a function, method-pattern hits outside a class, and non-container nesting, and qualifies names with the Go receiver or enclosing class. Scores use `branchCount` divided by length, weighted by `log10(length + 1)`.

sections.title: keyFunctions
sections.explanation: Filters to callables of sufficient length, excluding constructors (`constructor`, `__init__`, `new`), and sorts by score, then by length, then by position, keeping the top five.

sections.title: Finding where a declaration ends
sections.explanation: `codeOf` strips comment lines and trailing comments but keeps string literals so template-literal braces balance. `endOf` scans up to ten header lines: a trailing `:` means an indentation-based body (Python); a trailing `{` starts brace counting to the matching close; a `;` or one-line `}` ends it immediately. Otherwise the end is the last line still indented deeper than the declaration, ignoring blank lines and allowing closing brackets. `trimBlank` trims trailing blank lines on unbalanced braces.

src/atlas/links.ts.overview: Computes the Atlas links, purely from code and git history with no model involved: which described files import which, and which files change together in commits. Results are cached in `.fiu/links.json` keyed by HEAD and file hashes. These links feed the 'Around this code' section and the Debrief later in the tour (Step 11).

sections.title: Co-change and hub thresholds
sections.explanation: `CO_CHANGE` sets how many commits are read, ignores commits touching more than 20 files (renames, formatting, lockfile bumps), and requires at least 3 shared commits and a 0.3 ratio, keeping 5 partners. `HUB` marks files that change with so many others that co-change says nothing, calibrated on Fiu's own history.

sections.title: Links schemas
sections.explanation: Zod schemas describe a co-change partner (path, shared commits, ratio over the less-frequently-changed file), per-file links (imports, importedBy, changesWith, commit count), and the cached file with its cache `key`, commits read and hubs. `NO_LINKS` is the empty default.

sections.title: loadLinks with caching
sections.explanation: Builds a cache key from HEAD (or `no-commits`) plus every described file's path and blob hash, and returns the cached links if they match. Otherwise it reads sources for files whose profile has an import style, computes the import graph and co-change, and writes the result atomically via a temp file and rename, only if the `.fiu` directory exists.

sections.title: importGraph
sections.explanation: Dispatches each source to the resolver for its import style, drops self-imports, and builds both directions. A Go import names a package folder (trailing `/`), so every file in that folder is marked as imported by the importer.

sections.title: Relative (JS/TS) imports
sections.explanation: Matches `from`, dynamic `import(...)` and `require(...)` with relative specifiers. Each is resolved against the importer's folder and tried as-is, with TypeScript's `.js`-means-`.ts` mapping, with each script extension appended, and as an `index` file. Only targets in the described file set count.

sections.title: Python imports
sections.explanation: Resolves absolute modules from the repository root and from every ancestor folder of the file, supporting `src/` layouts and scripts on `sys.path`. Relative imports climb by dot count. For `from a import b`, if `a` is a package `__init__.py` it also tries `a/b.py` since `b` may be a submodule.

sections.title: Go imports
sections.explanation: `readGoModules` finds every tracked `go.mod` and sorts modules longest name first so nested modules win. `goImports` collects import specs from blocks and single lines, maps those under a known module to a folder, and keeps folders that contain Go files other than the importer's own.

sections.title: coChange
sections.explanation: Reads `git log` with a record separator per commit and file names only, skipping merges, renames and mass commits. It counts commits per file and per sorted pair, then keeps pairs above the shared and ratio thresholds in both directions. Hubs are files whose partner count reaches the larger of 5 or a third of changed files; each list is sorted by shared commits, ratio and path, and trimmed to five.

src/atlas/describe.ts.overview: The model-facing half of the Atlas: it builds the prompt for one folder (or a slice of its files), defines the structured output schema, checks the model's answer against strict length and naming rules, and saves accepted descriptions tied to content hashes. The same prompt rules and checks are shared with agent mode, so descriptions are validated identically whoever writes them (Step 11).

sections.title: Limits and output schema
sections.explanation: Sets line-length and line-count limits so every Atlas line fits beside a name in `fiu map`, caps key function bodies shown at 80 lines, and describes up to 10 files per call. `AtlasOutputSchema` is the Zod schema for the folder entry plus per-file text and per-key-function lines.

sections.title: ATLAS_RULES system prompt
sections.explanation: The system prompt shared by Fiu's API calls and agent mode's `prepare_atlas`. It explains the bottom-up order, asks for plain descriptions of purpose using domain concepts rather than syntax, forbids guessing or judging quality, and states the per-entry length rules.

sections.title: Building the folder prompt
sections.explanation: `folderPrompt` lists the folder, its subfolders with existing entries, other files (marking tests and generated files), then a section per file to describe, ending with the instruction appropriate to whether the folder entry or repository overview is wanted. `fileSection` lists declarations with line ranges and includes the code of each key function, or the first 40 lines when there are none, truncated by `codeLines`.

sections.title: Checking model output
sections.explanation: `checkAtlasOutput` returns a list of problems: empty or overlong folder, file and function entries; files that were not asked for or are described twice; function names that do not match a declared symbol; missing key functions; and undescribed files. An empty list means the output can be saved. Agent mode reuses this as its submit check.

sections.title: Applying output to the Atlas
sections.explanation: `applyAtlasOutput` tidies whitespace and writes file entries with the skeleton's blob hash, and the folder entry with the folder's names hash when wanted. Tying each entry to a hash is what later lets the store mark it current or stale.

sections.title: describeFolder with one retry
sections.explanation: Makes a structured `generateText` call with the rules and schema. If the checks find problems, the model's response and a correction message listing them are appended and it tries once more. `NoObjectGeneratedError` is treated as a retryable unusable answer, while other errors propagate; token usage is collected across both attempts for cost tracking.

src/atlas/store.ts.overview: Persists the Atlas in `.fiu/atlas.json` and provides the bookkeeping around it: schema validation, atomic writes, current/stale/missing state by hash, per-folder work planning, stale counts, and merging two Atlases for sharing and fetching. It also ensures entries read from Understand-Anything's output are never saved as Fiu's own (Step 11).

sections.title: Atlas schemas
sections.explanation: An entry stores the hash of what was described, its text and when it was written; file entries add one line per key function. The optional `source: 'understand-anything'` marks entries read from another tool, kept only in memory. The root folder key `''` holds the repository overview.

sections.title: Reading and writing
sections.explanation: `readAtlas` returns an empty Atlas when the file is absent and filters out foreign entries after parsing. `ownEntries` drops anything with a `source`. `writeAtlas` writes only own entries, with keys sorted for stable diffs, atomically through a temp file and rename.

sections.title: Entry state and folder work
sections.explanation: `entryState` compares a stored hash to the current one: missing, current or stale. `folderWork` lists a folder's described files that are not current, and says the folder entry needs writing whenever any file does or its own names hash changed. `staleCounts` totals stale files and folders plus how many files have any description.

sections.title: Merging Atlases
sections.explanation: `mergeAtlas` copies the base, adds entries only the incoming side has, and for conflicting entries (different hash or text) asks a `pick` strategy. It reports how many entries were added and replaced.

sections.title: Merge strategies
sections.explanation: `preferOursOrNewer` is used when sharing: the sharer's entry wins for the same content, otherwise the more recently written one. `preferCurrent` is used when fetching: a fetched entry replaces a local one only when the local entry is stale and the fetched one matches the code as it is here.

src/workouts/context.ts.overview: Builds the `Around this code` section saved with every Workout: what surrounds the target file (folder and file descriptions from the Atlas, plus import and co-change links), never the target itself. It is assembled from a template with no model call, and its central job is spoiler prevention: any description that names the target functions, uses tokens only the changed lines contain, or echoes words that distinguish the right answer is dropped. It belongs to the tour step on Around This Code and Debriefs, and its `otherVersions` and `targetNames` helpers are reused by the Debrief.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Pulls together the Atlas pieces (skeleton, links, overlay, store, symbol extraction), the diff utility and `buildVariant` from the Verified gate. The mix shows this module sits at the junction of the Atlas and Workout synthesis: it reads descriptions and links, and re-derives Variants to know what the Workout changes.

sections.title: Section shape and labels
sections.explanation: `AroundThisCode` is just Markdown lines plus a `dropped` count, so callers can report how many descriptions were suppressed for leaking. `PER_ROW = 3` caps each link row so the section stays orientation rather than homework. The `MODEL_WORD*` footers are honest provenance labels: descriptions are a model's word, not Verified, with a distinct variant when some came from Understand-Anything. `COMMON` lists generic code words that would cause false-positive leak matches.

sections.title: Options and other versions
sections.explanation: `AroundOptions` carries everything needed to detect leaks: the Reference Solution, every other version of the code, and for Predictions or Diagnoses the true and wrong answer texts. `otherVersions` reconstructs those versions per kind: a Drill or Kata's starting code, each Diagnosis Cause's Variant, or each wrong Prediction option's Variant (or the previous code for an old-behaviour option). `answerTexts` splits choices into truth and wrong, returning undefined when nothing is marked correct.

sections.title: Assembling the section
sections.explanation: `aroundThisCode` builds the skeleton, reads the Atlas overlay and links, then diffs the Reference Solution against every other version to get hunks. A combined `leaks` predicate filters each description; leaking ones increment `dropped` instead of appearing. A Prediction never shows the file's own entry, because the entry summarises behaviour and the answer is behaviour. Link rows list `Used by`, `Uses` and `Changes with` (excluding hub files), and the footer label is chosen by whether any descriptions survived and whether any came from UA.

sections.title: Finding the target names
sections.explanation: The target is the requested `#symbol` plus every callable symbol whose line span overlaps a changed hunk. Each name is added with its last dotted segment too (when at least four characters), because prose about `Queue.push` usually just says `push`. Exported so the Debrief can identify the same target after the Attempt.

sections.title: Distinctive tokens of the change
sections.explanation: Collects what only the changed lines say: identifiers of four or more characters that appear nowhere else in the Reference Solution, numbers other than 0 and 1, and string literal contents. Comment-only lines are excluded since they change no behaviour and their prose would match almost any description. The idea is that shared vocabulary of the unit gives nothing away, while unique tokens could hint at the bug or the answer.

sections.title: Leak and answer matchers
sections.explanation: `answerPicker` finds the stemmed words used only by the true option (via the Atlas search `words` tokenizer) and flags any description containing one. `leakChecker` compiles case-insensitive word-boundary regexes for every name and token, in both raw and spoken form (`maxRetries` also matches `max retries`). Both return predicates, so the cost of building patterns is paid once per section.

src/workouts/debrief.ts.overview: Computes and renders the Debrief shown after an Attempt finishes: where the code lives, what the target functions are for, who calls them, computed tension signals, and up to three `Try next` commands. Unlike `Around this code`, it is computed at display time from today's code, Atlas and links, since there is nothing left to spoil. It is part of the Around This Code and Debriefs tour step and reuses `otherVersions` and `targetNames` from context.ts.

sections.title: Debrief model and limits
sections.explanation: The `Debrief` interface is a plain data structure separate from rendering, with fields for anchors, target descriptions, callers, signals and suggestions, plus flags for a changed source and UA provenance. `DebriefOptions.profiles` being absent means context is off, in which case the Debrief only says where the code lives. `TRY_NEXT` and `LISTED` keep output short.

sections.title: Target and callers
sections.explanation: `buildDebrief` returns early with only anchors when context is off or the file no longer exists in the skeleton. It finds target functions, attaches Atlas function descriptions, and records whether the file entry came from UA. Callers are found by reading each importing file and testing for the target's last name segment with a word-boundary regex, so `Used by` can be refined to who actually calls the target.

sections.title: Tension signals and suggestions
sections.explanation: Signals are computed, never a model's word: blast radius from importers, churn from recent commits, hidden coupling (files that change together without importing each other, hubs excluded), and hub status. `Try next` proposes concrete commands: predict a caller, diagnose a hidden-coupling partner, drill a dependency. The `suggest` helper dedupes by target path and caps the list, and a comment notes that What-if sentences are deliberately avoided because they would need a model.

sections.title: Locating the target
sections.explanation: `findTarget` first re-reads the saved Workout files, rebuilds the other versions and diffs them to find changed functions, keeping only names the current file still has. If that yields nothing (or files are missing), it falls back to the `#symbol` plus callables overlapping today's Source Anchors. `innermost` drops an enclosing class when one of its methods is also a target, so the Debrief names the most specific function.

sections.title: Rendering helpers
sections.explanation: Small helpers for pluralising, truncated lists, provenance notes and the UA mark. `calling` phrases the callers compactly: `all call x` when every importer calls the single target, otherwise a list of path-to-function pairs. It takes a `code` formatter so the same logic serves plain text and Markdown backticks.

sections.title: Terminal rendering
sections.explanation: `renderDebriefText` emits indented sections only when they have content, and shows the source-changed warning only when there is context to which it applies. `Try next` commands are padded to a common width for an aligned table. The provenance note closes the Debrief whenever any context was shown.

sections.title: Markdown rendering
sections.explanation: `renderDebriefMarkdown` mirrors the terminal layout as `debrief.md` in the Attempt directory, with headings, bullet lists and inline code. Keeping two renderers over one data model lets each output format stay idiomatic without duplicating the computation.

src/atlas/ua.ts.overview: The only module that knows Understand-Anything's knowledge-graph format (ADR 0010). It reads the graph from `.understand-anything/` or `.ua/`, parses it defensively with Zod, resolves file and function nodes, layers and tour steps against Fiu's skeleton, and reports unreadable graphs instead of failing. The result is a `ForeignAtlas` that overlay.ts lays under Fiu's own Atlas, labelled as a model's word rather than Verified. It belongs to the Around This Code and Debriefs tour step.

sections.title: Location and limits
sections.explanation: The module comment sets the contract: UA's format is not a contract, so every field is optional and a bad graph is reported and ignored. `UA_DIRS` lists the legacy directory first so it wins when both exist, matching UA's own order. `MIN_MATCH_RATIO` and `MIN_NODES_TO_JUDGE` drive a heuristic warning that the format may have changed.

sections.title: Foreign Atlas types
sections.explanation: `ForeignFile` holds a file's sentence, tags, layer and function sentences keyed by Fiu symbol names, plus the blob hash at the analysed commit. `ForeignAtlas` adds layers, tour steps, the overview, and counts used for diagnostics. `ForeignAtlasResult` is a discriminated union (`absent`, `unreadable`, `read` with optional warning) so callers handle each case explicitly.

sections.title: Lenient schemas
sections.explanation: Zod schemas cover only the fields Fiu uses. The top-level `GraphSchema` keeps `nodes`, `layers` and `tour` as `unknown[]` with `.catch(undefined)`, so one malformed section does not invalidate the rest; each item is validated individually later. `CODE_TYPES` restricts matching to file, function and class nodes.

sections.title: Reading the graph
sections.explanation: `findUaDir` checks which directory contains `knowledge-graph.json`. `readForeignAtlas` turns JSON or I/O errors into an `unreadable` status with a reason, requires a nodes list, and, when the graph records a commit, fetches blob hashes at that commit so staleness can be judged per file. The pure resolution step is delegated to `resolveGraph`.

sections.title: Resolving code nodes
sections.explanation: `resolveGraph` is pure so it can be tested on any graph. Each node is parsed individually, counting skipped ones. File nodes contribute a first-sentence summary and merged, deduplicated tags; function and class nodes are mapped to a skeleton symbol via `symbolOf` and stored as function sentences. Nodes whose path is not in the skeleton are counted but ignored, which feeds the match-ratio check.

sections.title: Layers, tour and result
sections.explanation: `filesOf` maps node IDs to skeleton file paths, falling back to parsing the ID when the node itself is missing. Layers record their files and assign the first layer to each file with `??=`. Tour steps default their order to position, drop steps with no resolvable files, and are sorted. A warning is attached when enough code nodes were seen but fewer than 20 percent matched.

sections.title: Staleness and path helpers
sections.explanation: `foreignState` reuses the Atlas `entryState` comparison: an entry without a known hash compares against an empty string, so it reads as stale. `kindOf` falls back to the ID prefix when `type` is missing, `normalise` converts paths to the skeleton's forward-slash form, and `pathOfId` extracts the path from `file:<path>` or `<kind>:<path>:<name>` IDs.

sections.title: Symbol matching and sentences
sections.explanation: `symbolOf` tries the node name and ID tail as exact skeleton symbol names, then accepts a last-segment match only when it is unique, so ambiguous names are not guessed. `firstSentence` flattens whitespace, cuts at the first sentence end, and truncates to the Atlas's 200-character limit on a word boundary with an ellipsis.

sections.title: Blob hashes at a commit
sections.explanation: Validates the commit string as hex before passing it to git, then runs `git ls-tree -r -z` and parses blob lines into a path-to-hash map. Any failure (commit not in this clone, shallow clone) returns undefined, which downstream marks every UA entry as stale rather than erroring.

src/atlas/overlay.ts.overview: Merges Fiu's own Atlas with Understand-Anything's graph into the Atlas Fiu shows (ADR 0010). Fiu's current entries always win; a UA entry fills in where Fiu has none, or replaces a stale one when UA's is current. It also produces the `build` view used to plan `fiu atlas build` and the `savable` function that guarantees UA entries never get written into Fiu's Atlas file. Part of the Around This Code and Debriefs tour step.

sections.title: Overlay types and labels
sections.explanation: `AtlasOverlay` exposes three Atlases: `atlas` (what is shown), `own` (Fiu's alone) and `build` (what planning uses), plus UA tags and layers as extra search words and a `UaStatus`. `UaStatus` extends the foreign result union with `off` and an optional `behind` commit count. `UA_LABEL`, `UA_MARK` and `fromUa` give every consumer one consistent way to label UA-sourced text.

sections.title: Reading the overlay
sections.explanation: `uaEnabled` reads the repo config's `understandAnything` flag, defaulting to on even if the config is unreadable, since other parts of Fiu report config errors. `readAtlasOverlay` short-circuits to Fiu's own Atlas when UA is off or not readable; otherwise it computes how far behind HEAD the analysed commit is and builds the overlay. The `build` Atlas combines Fiu's folder entries with the shown file entries, so a file with a current UA entry needs no new description.

sections.title: Merge rules
sections.explanation: `overlayAtlas` is pure. For each UA file it records tags and layer, then replaces Fiu's entry only when Fiu's is missing, or stale while UA's is current. Whole file entries come from one source, so the `source` label applies to their function descriptions too. The repository overview is handled separately: UA's project description is treated as current whenever its commit is in the clone, because it describes the project rather than a list of names.

sections.title: Saving and coverage
sections.explanation: `savable` prepares the build Atlas for `writeAtlas`: every UA entry is swapped back for Fiu's own entry (even a stale one) or removed, so Fiu's file never contains foreign text and planning around UA never loses Fiu's work. `coveredByUa` counts described files within a scope that are current only thanks to UA, used to tell the user how many files a build skipped.

sections.title: Notice and commit distance
sections.explanation: `uaNotice` produces one line explaining that UA's graph is in use (directory, short commit, how far behind or not in the clone), how to turn it off, and any format warning; or why it was ignored. `commitsBehind` uses `git rev-list --count` with `reject: false`, returning undefined on any failure rather than throwing.

src/commands/atlas.ts.overview: Implements the `fiu atlas` commands: `build` (describe missing or stale folders and files with a model, bottom up, after consent and a cost confirmation), `search` (local, free goal search over the Atlas with map states), and the plain view of the repository, a folder or a file with its links. All three read the Atlas through the UA overlay, so files with a current Understand-Anything description are skipped by builds and labelled in views. It appears in the Around This Code and Debriefs tour step.

sections.title: Imports and command types
sections.explanation: Imports span the Atlas modules, consent, credentials, cost estimation and the model factory. `AtlasDependencies` allows injecting `createModel`, config environment and a clock for tests. `AtlasCall` is one model call: a batch of a folder's files, with the folder's own entry requested on its last call. `AtlasBuildResult` reports how many files UA already covered in every outcome.

sections.title: Planning and estimating calls
sections.explanation: `planAtlasCalls` walks folders deepest first so a folder's description can draw on its children, batching files by `FILES_PER_CALL` and adding a folder-only call when no files need work. `estimateAtlasCost` approximates tokens at four characters each plus fixed per-entry output allowances. `lighter` lowers Anthropic effort to `low`, since describing is lighter work than designing Workouts.

sections.title: Build setup and scope
sections.explanation: `buildAtlas` prepares the workspace, resolves config and builds the skeleton and scope. It reads the overlay's `build` Atlas, so files with a current UA entry produce no calls and cost no tokens, and counts them with `coveredByUa`. When nothing needs describing it returns `up-to-date` before any API key is needed.

sections.title: Key, consent and cost check
sections.explanation: A missing API key error is enriched with the alternative of building the Atlas through a coding agent. Consent to send code to the provider is asked once and recorded; `--yes` bypasses prompts. Without `--yes`, the actual prompts are built to estimate cost, and the confirmation mentions how many files were skipped thanks to UA.

sections.title: Describing folder by folder
sections.explanation: Each call goes through `describeFolder`; spend is recorded per call so costs are tracked even if later calls fail. Failed calls are collected rather than aborting the build. Successful output is applied to the in-memory build Atlas and written immediately through `savable(atlas, own)`, which strips UA entries, so progress survives interruption and Fiu's file never stores foreign text.

sections.title: Atlas search command
sections.explanation: `searchAtlasCommand` is local and free: it searches the overlay Atlas, passing UA tags and layers as extra search words, and joins each result with its comprehension-map state from `buildMap`. It also reports whether any descriptions exist, which callers use to explain that only names are searched before a build.

sections.title: Atlas view
sections.explanation: `atlasView` resolves the given path relative to the repository. A file path yields a file view including its links; anything else yields a folder or repository scope view. The UA notice is attached when relevant so the renderer can disclose the graph's provenance.

src/commands/explore.ts.overview: Implements `fiu explore`: building a Track, a short ordered learning path of three to five Workouts through one module. It picks the module (by path or, with `--about`, through Atlas search), shortlists logic-dense files, makes one planning model call, confirms an estimated cost, then generates every step up front, replacing failed steps with alternates. It is the main entry of the Tracks, Map and Stats tour step.

sections.title: Options and results
sections.explanation: `ExploreOptions` covers consent, choosing a module by goal (`about`), overriding allowed kinds and disabling the sandbox. `ExploreResult` distinguishes a saved Track, too few Verified steps (the generated Workouts remain ordinary Workouts), a failed plan, and a declined confirmation.

sections.title: Choosing a module by goal
sections.explanation: `moduleAbout` sums search scores per folder over the top results, then for each folder in descending score walks up toward the root until it finds one whose shortlist has at least `MIN_STEPS` files. If nothing qualifies, the error hint depends on whether the Atlas has descriptions: without them only names are searched.

sections.title: Module and candidates
sections.explanation: `explore` resolves the module, rejecting paths outside the repository or inside `.fiu`. After config and API key resolution (with an agent-mode hint when the key is missing), it shortlists candidate files and enriches them with Atlas descriptions via `withAtlas`, read through the UA overlay. A module with fewer than `MIN_STEPS` candidates is refused with a suggestion to drill a single file.

sections.title: Consent, plan and estimate
sections.explanation: Consent is requested once per provider. The planning call (`planTrack`) has its spend recorded even when it fails. The cost estimate uses the user's recent average spend per kind, falling back to the overall average, and is reported as unknown without history. The confirmation lists each planned step with its kind, pillar, path and why line.

sections.title: One shared sandbox
sections.explanation: A single sandbox is opened lazily for the whole Track and verified once with the canary; each language toolchain is preflighted only the first time it is needed. This avoids repeating expensive sandbox setup for every step.

sections.title: Generating steps with fallbacks
sections.explanation: Each planned step is generated through `generateWorkout` as a single question tagged with Track metadata. On failure or a not-worth-practising verdict, the step is replaced by the next alternate (taking the planned step's kind), and finally by a Drill on the planned file if Drills are allowed. The sandbox is disposed in `finally`. With fewer than `MIN_STEPS` saved steps no Track is created; otherwise the Track record is saved.

sections.title: Recording plan spend
sections.explanation: A hoisted inner function records the planning call's cost as a `track-plan` spend entry with origin `explore`. Declared at the end but usable earlier thanks to function hoisting, it closes over `paths`, `module` and `config`.

src/explore/plan.ts.overview: Plans a Track with one inexpensive model call: it defines the structured plan schema, the system rules for ordering steps foundations first, the candidate prompt, and a validator that checks the plan against the shortlist and allowed kinds. The same rules are shared with agent mode's `prepare_track`. Part of the Tracks, Map and Stats tour step.

sections.title: Allowed kinds and limits
sections.explanation: `trackKinds` decides which Workout kinds a Track may use: an explicit `--kinds` override wins; otherwise, if the user's preferences are only no-code kinds (they do not read code), exactly those; else all four. `MIN_STEPS`, `MAX_STEPS` and `MAX_ALTERNATES` bound the plan.

sections.title: Plan schema and kind blurbs
sections.explanation: Zod schemas with `.describe()` annotations double as model instructions for structured output: each step has a path, kind, pillar (algorithm, pattern or library) and a why line. `TRACK_KINDS` gives the usual arc order, and `KIND_LINES` explains each kind and where it fits in a Track.

sections.title: Ordering rules prompt
sections.explanation: `trackRules` builds the system prompt: choose distinct files, order foundations first, skip glue, and assign kind, pillar and a role-only why line that never reveals a bug or answer. With several kinds allowed it requires at least two and suggests an arc from Prediction to Kata; with one kind it states every step uses it.

sections.title: Candidate prompt and Atlas
sections.explanation: `candidatesPrompt` lists each candidate with its line count and either its Atlas description or its declaration outline, indented beneath. `withAtlas` attaches the Atlas file text and function descriptions to candidates that have an entry, which gives the planner meaning instead of bare signatures.

sections.title: Validating a plan
sections.explanation: `checkPlan` returns human-readable problems: empty title, wrong step count, too many alternates, unknown or duplicate paths, empty why lines, disallowed kinds, and a single kind used when several are allowed. These strings are fed back to the model verbatim, so they are phrased as corrections.

sections.title: Planning call with retry
sections.explanation: `planTrack` calls `generateText` with structured output for up to two attempts. Usage is collected from successes and from `NoObjectGeneratedError` failures alike so cost is accounted. When the plan has problems, the model's response and a correction message listing them are appended to the conversation, letting the retry fix its own answer. Other errors propagate.

src/explore/shortlist.ts.overview: Produces a static, model-free shortlist of a module's most logic-dense source files for Track planning, and exports `logicScore`, the language-neutral measure also used by `fiu map` to colour never-practised files. Each candidate carries a short declaration outline so the planning call can see what a file is about without reading it all. Part of the Tracks, Map and Stats tour step.

sections.title: Candidate and heuristics
sections.explanation: `Candidate` holds path, language profile, size, score, outline and optional Atlas text. `BRANCHING` is a single regex of branching and error-handling keywords and operators across supported languages, a cheap proxy for logic. `DECLARATION` recognises declaration lines in several languages for the outline. `ExploreTargetError` marks user-facing target problems.

sections.title: Building the shortlist
sections.explanation: Validates that the module exists and is a directory, then lists only git-tracked files so local build output is ignored. Files that are not drillable, have no supported language profile, cannot be read or fall outside the size window are skipped. The rest are scored, given up to 12 trimmed declaration lines, sorted densest first and capped at `SHORTLIST_SIZE`.

sections.title: Logic score and paths
sections.explanation: `logicScore` is branches per line multiplied by `log10(lines)`, gently favouring larger files so a tiny helper does not tie a substantial module on density alone. Files under 15 lines or over the synthesis maximum return undefined. `repoRelativeDir` converts an absolute path to a forward-slash repository-relative path.

src/map/map.ts.overview: Implements `fiu map`, the comprehension-debt map: every tracked source file is coloured red, amber, green or grey from local signals only (logic scores, the user's Attempts, staleness since practice, recent AI-authored changes, Blind Spots), grouped by directory, and paired with up to three suggestions. When an Atlas exists (Fiu's or Understand-Anything's), it adds descriptions and staleness counts. Part of the Tracks, Map and Stats tour step.

sections.title: States and thresholds
sections.explanation: `FileState` is ordered worst first, with `SEVERITY` used for sorting and directory roll-up. Practice goes stale after 20 changed lines; AI changes count when within 30 days. Red and amber thresholds are quantiles of this repository's own logic scores, so colouring is relative rather than absolute.

sections.title: Report types
sections.explanation: `FileEntry` records state plus why: practice outcome and kinds, stale distance, AI change, score, a waiting Workout, an Atlas note and a Blind Spot. `AtlasNote` carries an optional `source` to label UA entries. `Suggestion` is a union of four actions, and `MapReport` optionally includes Atlas overview and stale counts.

sections.title: Scoring sources
sections.explanation: `buildMap` lists tracked files, keeps those with a language profile, and scores the drillable ones. Quantile thresholds are computed repo-wide regardless of scope. It then gathers practice by file, Blind Spots, recently AI-changed files and Workouts already waiting in the queue.

sections.title: Classifying each file
sections.explanation: A nested ternary encodes the colour rules: practised files are green, or amber when stale; never-practised files without a score are grey, those above the red threshold are red, and AI-changed files above the amber threshold are amber. Optional fields are spread in only when present, keeping JSON output compact.

sections.title: Attaching Atlas notes
sections.explanation: Building the skeleton reads every file, so it is done only when Fiu's Atlas file or a UA directory exists. Folder and file notes come from the overlay with a stale flag and source label. Stale counts are computed from the `build` Atlas, so files with a current UA entry are not reported as needing a refresh.

sections.title: Scope and practice history
sections.explanation: `normaliseScope` turns a cwd-relative path into a repository-relative scope. `practiceByFile` keeps, per source file, the latest finished outcome and its Workout's commit while accumulating every kind practised. It also folds in v1 outcomes recorded before Attempts existed, preserving older history. Note the duplicated doc comment above it.

sections.title: Git-derived signals
sections.explanation: `recentlyAiChanged` runs `git log` with record and unit separator characters in the format so commit messages and file lists can be split reliably, keeping files from AI-authored commits. `changedSince` sums added and removed lines from `git diff --numstat` against the practised commit, returning undefined when the commit is unknown.

sections.title: Grouping by directory
sections.explanation: Files are grouped by parent directory; each directory counts its colours and Blind Spots and takes the worst file state. Files within a directory are sorted worst first then by path, and directories alphabetically.

sections.title: Suggestions
sections.explanation: At most three suggestions in priority order: re-check Blind Spots, train Workouts already paid for on red or amber files, explore the directory with the most red files (at least two), then drill individual files not already covered or inside the explored module.

src/map/stats.ts.overview: Implements `fiu stats` and the Blind Spot logic shared with the map. It considers only the first finished Attempt at each Prediction or Diagnosis, since a retry already knows the answer, and reports accuracy overall, by kind, by confidence (calibration), over time and by directory. Part of the Tracks, Map and Stats tour step.

sections.title: Calibration constants and types
sections.explanation: `EXPECTED_RATE` sets what each confidence level should hit if the user's self-assessment is accurate (25, 70 and 95 percent). `MIN_ANSWERS` marks small samples as noise. `FirstAnswer`, `Tally`, `AnswerStats` and `BlindSpot` model the report.

sections.title: First answers and Blind Spots
sections.explanation: `firstAnswers` walks answer-only Workouts and takes the first finished Attempt, recording correctness and confidence, sorted oldest first. `blindSpots` keeps the latest first answer per file and flags those that were certain and wrong, so a later right answer on the same file clears the Blind Spot.

sections.title: Computing the stats
sections.explanation: `answerStats` filters answers to the scope, groups them by directory, and builds tallies per kind, per confidence level with its expected rate, for the last 30 days versus before, and per directory. Directories are sorted lowest accuracy first, so the weakest areas lead.

src/background/refill.ts.overview: Implements `fiu refill`, which turns a commit into a Quick Workout, either in the foreground or unattended from the post-commit hook. In the background it never prompts, holds a per-repository lock, queues commits that arrive meanwhile in a small backlog, obeys queue and daily caps, and logs every outcome to `.fiu/log`. It opens the Background Refill and Sharing tour step.

sections.title: Constants and types
sections.explanation: Defines the backlog size, the 30-minute stale lock threshold and how many processed commits are remembered. `RefillOptions` separates background behaviour (no prompts, always sandboxed, caps enforced) from foreground flags. `CommitOutcome` reuses the log entry shape, and `RefillBusyError` is thrown only in the foreground when another generator holds the lock.

sections.title: Setup and early refusals
sections.explanation: `refill` resolves config, auto settings and the commit SHA, and defines `note`, which records each outcome and appends it to the log without the bulky generation result. Expired queued Workouts are discarded first. In the background, generation is refused when auto mode is off or consent is missing; a missing API key is logged with a hint about GUI commits not seeing shell variables rather than thrown.

sections.title: Lock, sandbox and backlog loop
sections.explanation: If the lock is held, background runs add the commit to the backlog and return; foreground runs throw. The sandbox is opened lazily and reused. The loop processes the commit, then in the background keeps taking the newest backlog entry until it is empty. Sandbox disposal and lock release happen in `finally`.

sections.title: Filtering a commit
sections.explanation: `processCommit` skips already-processed commits and permanently skips merges, commits made during a rebase or similar, other authors' commits, and non-AI commits when `aiOnly` is set. A target file is chosen; a file that already has a queued commit Workout is skipped. Diagnoses are filtered out since commits do not become Diagnoses yet, and Predictions need the file before the commit. Background runs check queue and daily caps (deferring, not remembering); foreground runs ask for consent.

sections.title: Generating with kind fallback
sections.explanation: Tries each wanted kind in order: a Prediction is unfit when the commit added the file, and a not-worth-practising verdict falls through to the next kind. The remaining daily budget is rechecked before each attempt so fallbacks count against the cap. Saved or failed generations mark the commit processed. In the background, unexpected errors become a logged `failed` outcome; in the foreground they propagate to the user.

sections.title: Git helpers
sections.explanation: `backgroundRefusal` explains why unattended generation must not run. `fileBefore` uses `git show sha^:path` with `stripFinalNewline: false` to preserve exact content, returning undefined when the file did not exist. `resolveCommit` verifies the revision is a commit and returns its full SHA.

sections.title: Caps, expiry and state
sections.explanation: `countsTowardQueueCap` excludes Track steps from the background queue cap. `generationsToday` sums commit-origin generation attempts since local midnight, retries included. `expireStaleWorkouts` discards only the user's own queued commit Workouts past expiry, never shared ones. `markProcessed`, `addToBacklog` and `takeFromBacklog` keep bounded, deduplicated lists in state, with the backlog taken newest first.

sections.title: Per-repository lock
sections.explanation: `acquireLock` creates `refill.lock` with the exclusive `wx` flag, storing pid and timestamp. On `EEXIST` it inspects the holder: if the process is alive and the lock is younger than 30 minutes it gives up; otherwise it removes the lock and retries once. `isAlive` uses `process.kill(pid, 0)`, treating `EPERM` as alive because the process exists but belongs to another user.

src/background/auto.ts.overview: Implements `fiu auto on/off/status`: the opt-in background generation feature. It installs a marked block in the repository's git post-commit hook that launches `fiu refill --background` for each new commit, records consent and caps in `.fiu/config.json`, and reports the state of background generation. It is the switch half of tour step 14, while refill.ts does the actual per-commit work.

sections.title: Imports and hook markers
sections.explanation: Pulls in config defaults, consent recording, spend helpers from the Workout store and queue/daily counters from refill.ts. `BEGIN`/`END` delimit Fiu's block inside a hook file the user may also own, and `CREATED_BY_FIU` marks files Fiu created so that `auto off` knows it may delete them. `quote` is a POSIX single-quote escaper so paths with spaces or quotes survive in the shell hook.

sections.title: The hook block
sections.explanation: `hookBlock` builds the shell snippet. It runs the refill command in a subshell with `nohup ... &` and all streams redirected, so the commit never waits on generation. It first unsets git's commit-time variables (`GIT_INDEX_FILE`, `GIT_DIR`, ...) because they would otherwise redirect Fiu's own git calls into the in-progress commit's state.

sections.title: Install and remove the hook
sections.explanation: `installHook` honours `core.hooksPath`: when a managed hooks directory is configured it returns a `manual` result with the snippet instead of editing possibly tracked files. Otherwise it resolves the hook via `git rev-parse --git-path` (correct for worktrees), replaces any existing Fiu block and appends the new one, creating and chmod-ing the file only if it did not exist. `removeHook` strips exactly the block and deletes the file only if Fiu created it and nothing else remains.

sections.title: Legacy hook migration
sections.explanation: The project was previously named Fiutsu and Kintsugi; `migrateLegacyHook` finds a block written under either former marker pair and swaps it in place for the current block, also rewriting the 'created by' marker. User lines around the block are left untouched.

sections.title: Block text helpers
sections.explanation: `hookInstalled` checks for the begin marker. `removeBlock` slices out the text between the markers and normalises blank lines, and `appendable` ensures exactly one blank line before a newly appended block regardless of how the file ended.

sections.title: Config and caps
sections.explanation: `setAuto` edits the raw JSON config, preserving every other setting and stamping `consentedAt` when enabling. `autoCaps` resolves the effective queue cap, daily limit, AI-only flag and expiry from config over `AUTO_DEFAULTS`, deliberately ignoring other fields of the `auto` object.

sections.title: Status report
sections.explanation: `autoStatus` assembles what `fiu auto status` shows: whether it is enabled and the hook present, the caps, generations today, how many queued Workouts count toward the cap, whether generation is paused because the queue is full, the backlog length, and the last three failed background log entries.

sections.title: Enabling with consent
sections.explanation: `enableAuto` requires one explicit consent covering both background spending and sending code to the provider. Without `--yes` and without an interactive `confirm` it throws `AutoConsentRequiredError`; otherwise it shows the provider, model, caps and the average past Drill cost before asking. On acceptance it writes the config, records provider consent if it differs, and installs the hook.

src/background/commits.ts.overview: Commit inspection for background refill. It reads commit metadata, detects AI-co-authored commits from `Co-Authored-By` trailers, notices in-progress merges/rebases, and picks at most one drillable file per commit together with its source and diff. refill.ts (tour step 14) uses it to decide whether and what to turn into a Quick Workout.

sections.title: Commit info and AI detection
sections.explanation: `CommitInfo` carries sha, subject, author, parents and an `aiAuthored` flag. The `AI_CO_AUTHOR` regex matches a `co-authored-by:` line mentioning known coding assistants, case-insensitively and per line. `readCommit` uses a single `git show -s` with NUL-separated format fields so subjects and bodies cannot break the parse.

sections.title: Operations in progress
sections.explanation: `operationInProgress` looks for git's marker files (`rebase-merge`, `CHERRY_PICK_HEAD`, `MERGE_HEAD`, ...) in the git dir. Commits made during these operations replay existing changes, so refill can skip them; the function returns a human-readable name of the operation for the skip message.

sections.title: Size thresholds and target types
sections.explanation: `MIN_CHANGED_LINES` and `MAX_CHANGED_LINES` bound what counts as one focused change worth a Drill; the diff sent to the model is capped at `MAX_DIFF_LINES` while the whole file is always sent. `TargetChoice` is a discriminated union: either a target or a skip reason, so callers always get an explanation.

sections.title: Choosing the target file
sections.explanation: `chooseTarget` reads `git show --numstat --no-renames`, skips binaries, non-drillable paths (tests, generated, vendored) and files without a Language Profile, and takes the file with the most changed lines. It then rejects too-small or too-large changes and files deleted by the commit, and returns the file content at that commit plus a possibly truncated diff. `--no-renames` keeps every path a plain path.

src/sharing/share.ts.overview: Team sharing: `fiu share` publishes Workouts, whole Tracks or Series, and optionally the Atlas to a shared git branch, and `fiu fetch` imports what teammates shared. Identity is by content fingerprint, so the same Workout is never duplicated and id collisions get a suffix. Every incoming Workout is re-verified in the local sandbox before it is accepted, preserving the Verified rule from tour step 8.

sections.title: Imports and constants
sections.explanation: Draws on the Atlas store and skeleton, config, Tracks, the sandbox and Verified gate, the Workout store, and low-level git plumbing from `./git.ts`. The shared branch's layout is `workouts/<id>/...`, `tracks/<id>.json` and a single `atlas.json`. `PUSH_ATTEMPTS` bounds the optimistic retry loop when pushes race.

sections.title: Content fingerprint
sections.explanation: `stable` sorts object keys recursively so equal objects serialise identically. `fingerprint` hashes every file path and content, but strips `id` and `sharedBy` from `workout.json` first: what a Workout *is* does not depend on its name or who shared it, which is what makes deduplication and rename detection work.

sections.title: Reading local and shared trees
sections.explanation: `readDirFiles` loads a Workout directory into a path-to-Buffer map with forward-slash paths. `sharedContents` groups the shared commit's tree into Workouts and Tracks by prefix. `blobsToFiles` reads blobs, `hashContent` writes a blob with `git hash-object -w`, and `suffixed` builds a collision-free id from the fingerprint.

sections.title: Options, Atlas helpers, report
sections.explanation: `ShareOptions` names the remote and the `--atlas` flag. `sharedAtlas` treats an unparsable shared Atlas as absent rather than failing, and `atlasJson` serialises with sorted keys so blob hashes are stable and unchanged Atlases don't create commits. `ShareReport` records what was shared and under which id.

sections.title: share: resolving what to publish
sections.explanation: Each id is expanded as a Track (all its step Workouts), a Series (all its questions) or a single Workout, then deduplicated. Workouts made from uncommitted or dirty code are refused, since teammates could not see their source; commits not yet on any remote branch only produce a warning.

sections.title: share: building and pushing the commit
sections.explanation: Inside a retry loop it fetches the shared branch, skips Workouts already present with an equal fingerprint, suffixes ids that clash with different content, and stamps `sharedBy` (keeping a teammate's original stamp). Track manifests are rewritten to the shared ids. With `--atlas` the local Atlas is merged with the team's using `preferOursOrNewer`. A commit is built directly from blobs with `commitWith`; if the push loses a race, the loop starts again from the teammate's branch.

sections.title: Fetch types
sections.explanation: `FetchOptions.sandbox` mirrors `--no-sandbox`, which disables isolation only for this invocation. `FetchReport` lists imports (with their local ids), duplicates, rejections with reasons, imported and skipped Tracks, and Atlas entries added or replaced.

sections.title: fetchWorkouts: setup and lazy sandbox
sections.explanation: Ensures the workspace, resolves config and the remote, fetches the shared branch, and indexes local Workouts by id and by fingerprint so a renamed import is recognised next time. The sandbox is opened and canary-checked lazily, and each Language Profile is preflighted once, so a fetch with nothing new never spins up a sandbox.

sections.title: fetchWorkouts: re-verify and import
sections.explanation: For each incoming Workout not already present by fingerprint, it picks a non-colliding id, requires a matching local Language Profile, and re-runs the Verified gate on the shared starting code, solution and tests. Passing Workouts are staged under `.fiu/incoming` and moved into place with a single `rename`, which is atomic on the same filesystem.

sections.title: fetchWorkouts: Tracks, Atlas, cleanup
sections.explanation: Track manifests are imported only when every step maps to a local Workout, using the id remapping built above. The team Atlas is merged with `preferCurrent` against a fresh skeleton, so entries describing stale code don't overwrite current ones. The `finally` block always disposes the sandbox and removes the staging directory.

src/agent/mcp.ts.overview: Builds the `fiu mcp` server: Fiu's tools exposed over the Model Context Protocol so the user's coding agent can author Workouts, Tracks and Atlas entries. Each tool is a thin wrapper that validates input with Zod and delegates to `AgentDrills` (drills.ts). It is the entry point of tour step 15.

sections.title: Imports and agent-facing errors
sections.explanation: `AGENT_FACING_ERRORS` lists the error classes that represent something the agent can act on (wrong target, unsupported language, missing sandbox or toolchain, oversized source, not a git repo). These become MCP tool errors; anything else is treated as a real bug and rethrown. Tool descriptions and server instructions are imported from texts.ts so wording lives in one place.

sections.title: prepare_drill and submit_drill
sections.explanation: The server is created with `SERVER_INSTRUCTIONS`, which every MCP client receives. `prepare_drill` exposes kind, quick, afterTask, Track, What-if and Series parameters with descriptive Zod schemas, maps `afterTask` to the `agent-task` origin, and appends a stale-install notice when needed. `submit_drill` accepts either a single Workout or a Prediction Series schema and, on success, tells the agent the exact `fiu train` command to relay.

sections.title: Track and Atlas tools
sections.explanation: `prepare_track`/`finish_track` drive Track building, `prepare_atlas`/`submit_atlas` let the agent describe the repository folder by folder (reusing `AtlasOutputSchema` from describe.ts), `search_atlas` maps a learning goal to targets, and `list_workouts` returns the queue. All of them go through `respond`.

sections.title: respond and stale-install notice
sections.explanation: `respond` serialises a result as pretty JSON text content, or converts an agent-facing error into `isError: true` with the message, so the agent can read and adapt instead of the server crashing. `staleInstallNotice` compares the version stamped into the installed skill against the running Fiu and asks the agent to tell the user to reinstall when it is older.

src/agent/drills.ts.overview: `AgentDrills` is agent mode's core: the coding agent writes the Workout, and Fiu supplies the same system prompt, schema, Verified gate and sandbox used by its own generation, then saves the result. It keeps in-memory state for pending generations and Tracks across MCP calls, enforces submission caps and queue caps, and never runs Workout code unsandboxed. mcp.ts (tour step 15) is a thin layer over this class.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Brings together almost every pipeline stage seen earlier in the tour: Atlas preparation and search, target parsing from commands/drill.ts, config and Language Profiles, Track planning from explore/, the sandbox and canary, prompts and schemas from synthesis/, the Verified gate, and saving/spend recording from workouts/.

sections.title: Request and state types
sections.explanation: `AGENT_TASK_QUEUE_CAP` stops an agent that finishes many tasks from flooding the queue. `AgentRequestError` marks refusals the agent should act on. `Generation` is the per-generationId state (source as sent, kind, submissions used, optional Track, What-if and Series). `PendingTrack`, `PreparedTrack`, `Prepared` and the `Submitted` union define what the tools return.

sections.title: Class state and Track preparation
sections.explanation: Generations and Tracks live in private maps, and the sandbox is a lazily created promise. `prepareTrack` rejects modules outside the repo or inside `.fiu`, shortlists candidate files enriched with Atlas entries via `withAtlas`, requires at least `MIN_STEPS` candidates, and returns the same ordering rules Fiu's own planner uses, with Atlas text replacing outlines where available.

sections.title: Atlas tools and workspace helper
sections.explanation: `prepareAtlas`/`submitAtlas` delegate to atlas/agent.ts. `searchAtlas` turns search results into agent-friendly targets, annotating stale entries, Understand-Anything-sourced entries, a practice state label and over-long files. `#workspace` centralises repo root, workspace creation and config resolution.

sections.title: finishTrack
sections.explanation: Saves the Track only when at least `MIN_STEPS` steps were Verified; otherwise returns `not-enough` and the step Workouts remain ordinary Workouts. The pending Track is removed either way, so a trackId cannot be finished twice.

sections.title: prepare: validation and generation setup
